title: Session 3 — Biological Databases in code
section: One submitted record, two partner interfaces
text:
One submitted record, two partner interfaces
The submitted INSDC record V00497.1 is human beta-globin (HBB) mRNA, not a whole genomic region. Open it in the NCBI nucleotide interface and the ENA browser. The pages and file formats look different. Do they describe the same archived sequence?
The next cell retrieves this one small record through NCBI’s API in GenBank format and ENA’s API in EMBL format. It checks the full accession and sequence version, organism, length and sequence, rather than comparing only the title. No complete database download is needed.

import io
from datetime import datetime, timezone

archive_accession = "V00497.1"
archive_sources = {
    "NCBI": (
        "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi"
        "?db=nuccore&id=V00497.1&rettype=gb&retmode=text",
        "genbank",
    ),
    "ENA": (
        "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/api/embl/V00497.1?download=false",
        "embl",
    ),
}
archive_records = {}
for partner, (url, file_format) in archive_sources.items():
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
    response.raise_for_status()
    archive_records[partner] = SeqIO.read(io.StringIO(response.text), file_format)

def archive_taxon(record):
    return next(
        xref.split(":", 1)[1]
        for feature in record.features if feature.type == "source"
        for xref in feature.qualifiers.get("db_xref", [])
        if xref.startswith("taxon:")
    )

print("Retrieved (UTC):", datetime.now(timezone.utc).date())
print(f"{'Partner':8s} {'Accession.version':18s} {'Organism label':22s} {'Taxon':6s} Length (bases)")
for partner, archive_record in archive_records.items():
    print(f"{partner:8s} {archive_record.id:18s} "
          f"{archive_record.annotations['organism']:22s} {archive_taxon(archive_record):6s} {len(archive_record.seq)}")

ncbi_archive = archive_records["NCBI"]
ena_archive = archive_records["ENA"]
archive_checks = {
    "same accession.version": ncbi_archive.id == ena_archive.id == archive_accession,
    "same organism (taxonomy ID)": archive_taxon(ncbi_archive) == archive_taxon(ena_archive) == "9606",
    "same length": len(ncbi_archive.seq) == len(ena_archive.seq),
    "same sequence": str(ncbi_archive.seq).upper() == str(ena_archive.seq).upper(),
}
for check, passed in archive_checks.items():
    print(f"{check}: {passed}")
assert all(archive_checks.values()), "Inspect the two returned records before continuing."

Retrieved (UTC): 2026-10-30
Partner  Accession.version  Organism label         Taxon  Length (bases)
NCBI     V00497.1           Homo sapiens           9606   626
ENA      V00497.1           Homo sapiens (human)   9606   626
same accession.version: True
same organism (taxonomy ID): True
same length: True
same sequence: True


The organism labels have different formatting: Homo sapiens at NCBI and Homo sapiens (human) at ENA. Both source features identify taxon 9606. Comparing that identifier checks the organism without mistaking a common name in parentheses for a biological difference.
Check the evidence. These are two access routes to the same submitted record. Agreement checks retrieval and identity; it is not two independent experiments supporting the biological annotation. Read the record’s source, features, references and submission history before drawing biological conclusions. If a request fails, keep the accession and try another partner; do not interpret a failed link as evidence that the data never existed.
V00497.1 is an original submitted sequence. The NM_000518.5 RefSeq mRNA used below is a separate reference record. INSDC partners exchange submitted archival records; this does not make every NCBI resource, including RefSeq or Gene, an INSDC mirror. Nor should these two HBB mRNA accessions be assumed to have identical sequences without comparing them.

section: Linked records describe different parts of an investigation
text:
Linked records describe different parts of an investigation







Record role
What to check




Study / BioProject
Project description, purpose and links to its deposited data.


Sample / BioSample
Biological source, organism and recorded collection or treatment information.


Experiment
How the sequencing library was prepared and which instrument was used.


Reads / run
Sequence reads and their quality scores from a sequencing run.


Assembly / assembled sequence
A submitted reconstructed sequence, its assembly context and available annotation.



These roles link the context, source and data of an investigation. They are different from the DNA, RNA and protein levels followed in the next section. Some investigations have several samples and runs, and older sequence records may not link to every role. Follow the links actually present in a record; do not invent a project or read set for V00497.1. An archive stores a submitted assembly; receiving raw reads does not automatically assemble them.
Optional: follow a changing archive route. Inspect the metadata for run SRR9451988 at ENA and its experiment SRX6217698 at NCBI SRA. Its NISC trace-conversion history connects it to the older capillary Trace Archives discussed in the lecture. Find the organism, library label and sequencing technology. This example is Papio anubis (olive baboon), not human. The library label HBB alone does not demonstrate that every read covers the HBB gene; establishing that would require sequence comparison. Read sequences and quality scores in a current read archive do not by themselves establish that original chromatogram files are available through every interface. Inspecting metadata is sufficient here; do not download the full read set. The general habit is to retain the accession and follow the current archive route when an old website changes.

title: Session 3 — Biological Databases in code
text:
Read one supplied transcript record
The next identifier is supplied so we can concentrate on retrieval and interpretation: RefSeq transcript NM_000518.5, human HBB mRNA. This is a separate reference record from the submitted INSDC sequence compared above. We request one GenBank-format record, check the HTTP response and parse it with Biopython. The URL is printed so the request can be repeated outside Python.

transcript_accession = "NM_000518.5"
transcript_response = requests.get(
    "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi",
    params={"db": "nuccore", "id": transcript_accession, "rettype": "gb", "retmode": "text"},
    timeout=30,
)
transcript_response.raise_for_status()
mrna = SeqIO.read(io.StringIO(transcript_response.text), "genbank")

print("Source:", transcript_response.url)
print("Accession.version:", mrna.id)
print("Description:", mrna.description)
print("Organism:", mrna.annotations["organism"])
print("Recorded molecule type:", mrna.annotations["molecule_type"])
print("Transcript length:", len(mrna.seq), "bases")
print("First 60 bases:", mrna.seq[:60])
assert mrna.id == transcript_accession
assert mrna.annotations["organism"] == "Homo sapiens"
assert mrna.annotations["molecule_type"] == "mRNA"

Source: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=nuccore&id=NM_000518.5&rettype=gb&retmode=text
Accession.version: NM_000518.5
Description: Homo sapiens hemoglobin subunit beta (HBB), mRNA
Organism: Homo sapiens
Recorded molecule type: mRNA
Transcript length: 628 bases
First 60 bases: ACATTTGCTTCTGACACAACTGTGTTCACTAGCAACCTCAAACAGACACCATGGTGCATC



Inspect the annotation, including its links
The record describes mRNA although its sequence is written with T. DNA notation alone does not tell us whether a record represents genomic DNA, RNA or a physical cDNA experiment. Read the molecule type and annotation.
The gene feature links this transcript to a gene identifier. The CDS feature identifies its protein-coding region and linked protein accession. These are different kinds of identifier, even when one record includes them together. GenBank displays positions starting at 1 with both ends included. Biopython uses Python slice coordinates starting at 0 with the end excluded, so the code converts the start before printing.

gene_feature = next(feature for feature in mrna.features if feature.type == "gene")
cds_feature = next(feature for feature in mrna.features if feature.type == "CDS")
gene_links = [link for link in gene_feature.qualifiers.get("db_xref", [])
              if link.startswith("GeneID:")]
protein_accession = cds_feature.qualifiers["protein_id"][0]

print("Gene symbol:", gene_feature.qualifiers["gene"][0])
print("Linked gene identifier(s):", ", ".join(gene_links))
print("Linked protein accession:", protein_accession)
print("CDS on this transcript (1-based, inclusive):",
      int(cds_feature.location.start) + 1, "to", int(cds_feature.location.end))
assert "GeneID:3043" in gene_links
assert protein_accession == "NP_000509.1"

Gene symbol: HBB
Linked gene identifier(s): GeneID:3043
Linked protein accession: NP_000509.1
CDS on this transcript (1-based, inclusive): 51 to 494




Check what the coding region contains
A full mature mRNA includes untranslated regions (UTRs) as well as its CDS. Extract the CDS using its annotated location instead of translating the whole transcript or guessing where translation begins. For this complete, standard-code example, cds=True also checks the start codon, length and terminal stop codon. The stop codon is part of the CDS nucleotide span but does not add an amino-acid residue.

cds_sequence = cds_feature.extract(mrna.seq)
translation_table = int(cds_feature.qualifiers.get("transl_table", ["1"])[0])
translated_cds = cds_sequence.translate(table=translation_table, cds=True)
annotated_translation = cds_feature.qualifiers["translation"][0]

print("Full transcript:", len(mrna.seq), "bases")
print("CDS including terminal stop:", len(cds_sequence), "bases")
print("Bases outside the annotated CDS:", len(mrna.seq) - len(cds_sequence))
print("Encoded protein:", len(translated_cds), "residues")
print("Translated CDS matches the record's translation:",
      str(translated_cds) == annotated_translation)
assert str(translated_cds) == annotated_translation
assert len(cds_sequence) == 3 * (len(translated_cds) + 1)

Full transcript: 628 bases
CDS including terminal stop: 444 bases
Bases outside the annotated CDS: 184
Encoded protein: 147 residues
Translated CDS matches the record's translation: True


Interpret the checks. They confirm that we retrieved the requested record and interpreted its annotated coding region consistently. Comparing a computed translation with the same record’s annotation is a consistency check, not independent experimental confirmation.
Two transcripts, same gene? If a second transcript record links to GeneID:3043 in the same annotation context, that links it to the same annotated human gene. Distinct transcript accessions identify different records; sequence versions, source records and transcript variants need to be distinguished. The comparison above does not demonstrate alternative splicing in HBB. The lecture’s three-exon diagram illustrates possible mechanisms generally. In the lab, inspect the links and annotations of your selected records before deciding how they relate.

title: Session 3 — Biological Databases in code
text:
Parse one linked protein annotation
UniProt provides structured JSON as well as web pages. Here the supplied accession is P68871. Request only this entry and inspect selected fields. A shared gene name is insufficient to establish a particular transcript–protein relationship, so we also check its explicit RefSeq cross-references.

uniprot_response = requests.get("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P68871.json", timeout=30)
uniprot_response.raise_for_status()
entry = uniprot_response.json()
refseq_links = [link for link in entry.get("uniProtKBCrossReferences", [])
               if link["database"] == "RefSeq"]
linked_proteins = {link["id"] for link in refseq_links}
linked_transcripts = {prop["value"] for link in refseq_links
                      for prop in link.get("properties", [])
                      if prop["key"] == "NucleotideSequenceId"}

print("Source:", uniprot_response.url)
print("UniProt accession:", entry["primaryAccession"])
print("Entry type:", entry["entryType"])
print("Organism:", entry["organism"]["scientificName"])
print("Protein existence:", entry["proteinExistence"])
print("Our protein is explicitly cross-referenced:", protein_accession in linked_proteins)
print("Our transcript is explicitly cross-referenced:", transcript_accession in linked_transcripts)
assert entry["primaryAccession"] == "P68871"
assert entry["organism"]["taxonId"] == 9606
assert protein_accession in linked_proteins
assert transcript_accession in linked_transcripts

Source: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P68871.json
UniProt accession: P68871
Entry type: UniProtKB reviewed (Swiss-Prot)
Organism: Homo sapiens
Protein existence: 1: Evidence at protein level
Our protein is explicitly cross-referenced: True
Our transcript is explicitly cross-referenced: True



Read evidence attached to a particular claim
Reviewed status describes curation of an entry. The protein-existence field concerns evidence that the protein exists. Neither substitutes for the evidence attached to an individual functional claim. The next cell prints one function statement and its own evidence links. Read the linked source before deciding whether it supports the conclusion you want to make.

function_statement = next(text for comment in entry.get("comments", [])
                          if comment["commentType"] == "FUNCTION"
                          for text in comment.get("texts", []) if text.get("evidences"))
print("Function statement:", function_statement["value"])
for evidence in function_statement["evidences"]:
    print("Evidence:", evidence["evidenceCode"], evidence.get("source", ""), evidence.get("id", ""))
    if evidence.get("source") == "PubMed":
        print("Reference:", "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/" + evidence["id"] + "/")

Evidence: ECO:0000269 PubMed 28066926

title: Session 3 — Biological Databases in code
section: Optional: check a literature search through an API
text:
Optional: check a literature search through an API
Later in the lecture we use online literature searches. This example retrieves counts for two supplied terms and their Boolean combinations. It demonstrates query parameters, JSON parsing and a reasonableness check, rather than a complete literature review. Requests are spaced to respect NCBI’s unauthenticated rate limit and retried if the server asks us to slow down.

import time

def pubmed_count(term):
    for attempt in range(5):
        time.sleep(0.5)
        response = requests.get(
            "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi",
            params={"db": "pubmed", "term": term, "retmode": "json"}, timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            break
        time.sleep(2 * (attempt + 1))
    response.raise_for_status()
    return int(response.json()["esearchresult"]["count"])

a = pubmed_count("hemoglobin")
b = pubmed_count("malaria")
a_and_b = pubmed_count("hemoglobin AND malaria")
a_or_b = pubmed_count("hemoglobin OR malaria")
a_not_b = pubmed_count("hemoglobin NOT malaria")

print(f"hemoglobin              {a:>10,}")
print(f"malaria                 {b:>10,}")
print(f"hemoglobin AND malaria  {a_and_b:>10,}")
print(f"hemoglobin OR malaria   {a_or_b:>10,}   (predicted: {a + b - a_and_b:,})")
print(f"hemoglobin NOT malaria  {a_not_b:>10,}   (predicted: {a - a_and_b:,})")
print("OR count matches set arithmetic:", a_or_b == a + b - a_and_b)
print("NOT count matches set arithmetic:", a_not_b == a - a_and_b)

malaria                    125,734
hemoglobin AND malaria       4,470
hemoglobin OR malaria      410,914   (predicted: 410,914)
hemoglobin NOT malaria     285,180   (predicted: 285,180)
OR count matches set arithmetic: True
NOT count matches set arithmetic: True

Checks and next steps
The comparison of NCBI and ENA tested the identity of one shared submitted record. The transcript cells checked the requested molecule type, linked gene and protein, coding-region coordinates and translation. The JSON cells checked explicit links and displayed evidence for one claim. These checks illustrate how code can support careful reading of a record.
The literature counts should follow set union and set difference when the searches describe the same sets. If a live result differs, inspect PubMed’s query translation and repeat the requests; indexing can change between calls. Search counts change over time and do not measure the quality of the papers.

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.1 Learning goals
By the end of this session you should be able to:
Session 3 ended with two related sequences retrieved from the databases. This session asks the next question: which residues correspond to each other, and how much evidence does the alignment give for shared ancestry? An alignment is a hypothesis about that correspondence. It proposes which residues descend from the same ancestral position, so substitutions appear as aligned pairs, and insertions and deletions as gaps. The score of the alignment then says how plausible this proposed history is under the chosen scoring scheme. That is not the same as recovering the true evolutionary history, and much of this session is about the choices that go into the score.

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.2 Why alignment needs an algorithm
By definition, two sequences are homologous if and only if they share a common evolutionary origin. We cannot observe that ancestry directly, so we have to infer it from statistical evidence, usually the similarity (or identity) of the two sequences. Both measures require an alignment. Identity is the fraction of aligned positions with the same residue. Similarity is defined more loosely and also counts residues with shared physicochemical properties (two hydrophobic residues, say). High identity or similarity is therefore evidence for homology, not proof of it.
Since homology is defined by a common ancestor, it follows that homologs come in two kinds, depending on the event that separated them:

orthologs are homologs separated by a speciation event, such as myoglobin in human and in mouse;
paralogs are homologs separated by a gene duplication, such as α- and β-globin, which descend from a duplicated ancestral globin gene.

The two definitions refer to events, not to genomes, so paralogs need not be in the same genome. Human α-globin and mouse β-globin are paralogs too, because the duplication that separated the α- and β-globin genes happened before human and mouse diverged. Telling the two kinds apart therefore requires the order of events, and the section “From alignment to tree” below shows how a gene tree makes that order visible.
To measure identity, we first have to decide which residues to compare. When two sequences have the same length, this is trivial: we place one under the other and count the matches. Real sequences usually differ in length, because insertions and deletions have accumulated over evolutionary time. Where we place one sequence under the other then changes the answer dramatically. Two example globin sequences that are 21.5% identical when aligned correctly can look as low as 4% identical if placed naively. Finding the right placement is therefore the real problem.
Could we simply try every possible placement and keep the best one? Unfortunately not. For two sequences of length \(n\), allowing gaps, the number of possible alignments grows so fast that for \(n = 100\) it is already around \(10^{59}\), far too many to search exhaustively. This is why dynamic programming algorithms are used for this problem. They find the guaranteed-optimal alignment without ever checking most of the possibilities. The trick is that many candidate alignments share the same beginnings. Dynamic programming therefore solves the best alignment of every pair of prefixes once, stores it, and reuses it. Before we turn to the algorithm, it helps to see what a good alignment looks like.

4.2.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Sequence homology: orthology, paralogy and the other relatedness terms, in more depth than needed here

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.3 Visualising alignments: dot plots
The simplest way to see whether two sequences are related is a dot plot, and it needs no algorithm at all. We put one sequence along each axis of a grid and mark a dot wherever the row and column residues match. A run of matches then lines up as a diagonal line, which the eye picks out immediately. A long alignment shows up as one long diagonal, a repeat as several parallel diagonals, and an inversion as a diagonal running in the opposite direction. A dot plot gives no score and no optimal alignment, so it is only a fast qualitative screen. It is still used today to visualise the output of real alignments (BLAST’s web output includes one), because a picture answers “is there a match here at all, and roughly where?” faster than a score does. To get an actual alignment, and a score for it, we need dynamic programming.

4.3.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Dot plot (bioinformatics) — filtering/windowing techniques for noisy real sequences, beyond the simple version above

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.4 Dynamic programming: Needleman-Wunsch and Smith-Waterman
Dynamic programming builds a matrix \(V\) with one extra row and column (for handling the sequence starts), fills it in using a simple rule, and then traces back through it to read off the best alignment. Each cell \(V(i,j)\) holds the score of the best alignment of the first \(i\) residues of one sequence with the first \(j\) residues of the other. It is filled as the best of three options: extending the alignment diagonally with a match or mismatch, or opening a gap from above or from the left.
\[
V(i,j) = \max \begin{cases} V(i-1,j-1) + s(x_i, y_j) \\ V(i-1,j) + g \\ V(i,j-1) + g \end{cases}
\]
Here \(s(x_i, y_j)\) is a substitution score (see below) and \(g\) is a gap penalty. In practice, filling one cell means computing all three candidates and keeping the largest. The figure shows this for cell \(V(1,1)\) of a pair of 13- and 12-residue sequences, with a gap penalty of \(g=1\):






Figure 4.1: Filling one cell, \(V(1,1)\), of the dynamic-programming matrix: all three candidates are computed and the largest is kept (gap penalty \(g=1\)).



Every other cell is filled in the same way, and only the numbers that go into the three candidates change. Worked example. The following case is small enough to do completely by hand. We align \(x =
\texttt{GCAT}\) against \(y = \texttt{GAC}\), with match \(= +1\), mismatch \(= -1\) and gap \(= -1\):



Table 4.1: The dynamic-programming matrix for aligning \(x = \texttt{GCAT}\) with \(y = \texttt{GAC}\) (match \(+1\), mismatch \(-1\), gap \(-1\)). The traceback path of the optimal alignment is in bold.

Tracing back from the bottom-right corner (score 0) along the cells in bold in Table 4.1 gives the optimal global alignment:
G C A T

Here G matches G, C is deleted, A matches A, and T is mismatched with C, for a total score of \(1 - 1 + 1 - 1 = 0\).
The same procedure works at the scale where it is actually used. The figure below shows two protein sequences of 12 and 13 residues, with the completed matrix and its full traceback path highlighted:






Figure 4.2: The completed Needleman-Wunsch matrix for two protein sequences of 12 and 13 residues, with the traceback path highlighted.



This algorithm, Needleman-Wunsch, produces a global alignment, in which the entire length of both sequences is forced into the result, gaps and all. Often, however, we want only the best-matching sub-region, that is, a local alignment. Smith-Waterman achieves this with one change to the same algorithm. Negative values in the matrix are reset to zero, and the traceback starts from the highest-scoring cell anywhere in the matrix (not necessarily the bottom-right corner) and stops as soon as it reaches a zero.
Which of the two to use is a biological choice, not just a mechanical one. Global alignment is the right choice when we expect the two sequences to correspond along most of their length, as two myoglobins do. Local alignment is the right choice when they may share only a part, such as one domain common to two large multidomain proteins, or a short motif inside a long sequence. Forcing a global alignment on such sequences buries the shared region under a long tail of meaningless gaps. How the gaps are penalised is therefore the next question.

4.4.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Needleman–Wunsch algorithm and Smith–Waterman algorithm — pseudocode and complexity analysis beyond what’s needed here

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.5 Gap penalties: linear vs. affine
So far \(g\) has been a single flat number charged per gap position, and this choice matters more than it might seem. A linear gap penalty, \(g(n) = n \times g_{\text{op}}\) for \(n\) consecutive gaps, charges the same total whether the gaps are spread out or bunched together. Evolutionary insertions and deletions often affect contiguous stretches of residues. It is therefore usually more realistic to charge more for opening a gap than for extending one. A linear penalty, in contrast, can produce implausible alignments that scatter single gaps throughout and break up motifs that are conserved as a block.
The fix is an affine gap penalty. It charges a larger cost \(g_{\text{op}}\) to open a new gap and a much smaller cost \(g_{\text{ext}}\) to extend an already open one (\(g_{\text{ext}} \ll
g_{\text{op}}\)):
\[
g(n) = g_{\text{op}} + (n-1) \times g_{\text{ext}}
\]
With this penalty, a single long gap costs less than the same number of gap positions scattered as many short gaps, which is the behaviour we want. The figure below makes this concrete. It shows the same two sequences aligned once with a linear penalty (top pair), where the gaps are scattered and break up the shared “QQW” motif, and once with an affine penalty (bottom pair), where the gaps are consolidated into contiguous stretches and “QQW” stays together:






Figure 4.3: The same two sequences aligned with a linear gap penalty (top pair) and with an affine gap penalty (bottom pair).




4.5.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Gap penalty — covers this in more depth, including the position-dependent variant shown at the bottom of the figure above, which is beyond what this course needs

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.6 Substitution matrices: PAM and BLOSUM
The other ingredient of the alignment score is the substitution score \(s(x_i, y_j)\). These scores are log-odds scores, the logarithms of probability ratios from Session 1. Roughly, the score of residues \(a\) and \(b\) is the log of how often they are aligned in related proteins, divided by how often they would pair by chance given how common each residue is. A positive score therefore means that the pair is seen more often among related sequences than expected by chance, and a negative score that it is seen less often. Conservative substitutions (K and R, I and V) consequently score positively. Session 5’s profiles use the same idea, one column at a time. Two families of substitution matrices dominate, and they differ in the data and the model they are built from:

PAM (Point Accepted Mutations; Dayhoff, Schwartz & Orcutt, 1978) is based on global alignments of closely related proteins and uses an explicit evolutionary model. The sequences are arranged into phylogenetic trees, ancestral sequences are inferred, and substitutions are counted along the branches of the tree. Matrices for larger distances (PAM250) are then extrapolated from the one for very short distances.
BLOSUM (BLOcks SUbstitution Matrix; Henikoff & Henikoff, 1992) is instead based on local, ungapped alignments of distantly related proteins. Substitution frequencies are counted directly from conserved blocks of real multiple alignments, with no phylogenetic tree and no extrapolation. Each BLOSUM matrix (BLOSUM45, BLOSUM62, BLOSUM80, …) is therefore derived independently of the others.

The two families are easy to confuse, because their numbering runs in opposite directions. A higher PAM number means a more distant comparison, so PAM250 suits more divergent sequences than PAM100. A higher BLOSUM number, in contrast, means a closer comparison, so BLOSUM80 suits more similar sequences than BLOSUM45.

4.6.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Point accepted mutation and BLOSUM — the full derivation of each matrix family, beyond the conceptual level above

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.7 Is the score significant?
Once a substitution matrix and gap penalties are chosen, every alignment gets a score. A high score alone, however, does not prove that two sequences are homologous. The raw score depends on the sequence lengths, the substitution matrix and the gap penalties, so there is no universal threshold for “good enough”. One intuitive way to calibrate it is to compare the observed score with the scores of the same sequences shuffled, or of unrelated sequences, aligned in the same way. If the real score is far above almost all of them, chance is an unlikely explanation.
For local alignments this comparison can be made precise. The best scores of unrelated sequences follow a known statistical distribution, an extreme-value distribution rather than a normal one. Database-search tools use this distribution to estimate an E-value, the number of hits this good expected by chance in a database of this size. Session 5 explains BLAST and E-values properly.

4.7.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Extreme value theory, in its general statistical form, beyond its use here

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.8 Multiple sequence alignment
So far we have aligned two sequences, but a protein family usually has many members, and aligning more than two sequences at once is harder than it looks. Exact dynamic programming extends to \(N\) sequences, but its cost grows exponentially with \(N\), so it becomes impractical for more than a few short sequences. Practical methods therefore combine three ideas:

Progressive alignment builds a guide tree from all pairwise distances, aligns the closest pair first, and then adds sequences (or already aligned groups) one at a time. Early decisions are never revisited, so an early mistake can persist (ClustalW is the classic example).
Iterative refinement starts from a progressive alignment and repeatedly re-aligns parts of it, keeping the changes that improve the score (as in MUSCLE).
Consistency uses the agreement among all the pairwise alignments as extra information. If A aligns with B and B with C at a position, a multiple alignment in which A also matches C there is preferred (as in T-Coffee).

Real tools often combine several of these ideas, and which works best depends on the number, length and divergence of the sequences.
The guide tree for progressive alignment is built by the kind of hierarchical clustering used on any distance matrix. Every sequence starts as its own cluster, the closest pair of clusters is merged repeatedly, and the process stops once only one cluster remains. The merge order is the order in which the sequences are aligned. The figure shows a small worked example: five toy sequences that are almost identical except for sequence 4, their pairwise Hamming-distance matrix, and the resulting guide tree. Sequence 4 merges in only at the very last step, which reflects how clearly it differs from the other four.






Figure 4.4: A guide tree for five toy sequences: the pairwise Hamming distances and the resulting order of merges.



A guide tree is only an ordering device for the alignment and not necessarily a phylogenetic tree. It is usually built by a quick method (UPGMA) that assumes all lineages evolve at the same rate, so a fast-evolving sequence can end up in the wrong place. The third discussion problem shows such a case. To infer how the sequences are actually related, we need a method built for phylogeny. The two kinds of tree look alike but answer different questions:



Table 4.2: A guide tree and a phylogenetic tree.

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.9 From alignment to tree
A phylogenetic tree proposes how sequences are related by descent. The quickest route from an alignment to a tree uses the same ingredient as a guide tree, a matrix of pairwise distances, but combines it with a method built for phylogeny. Neighbour joining is such a method, because it allows lineages to evolve at different rates, which UPGMA does not. A tree is read as follows:

The leaves are the sequences, and the internal nodes are inferred ancestors.
The branch lengths show the amount of change (here, the fraction of differing residues).
A clade is an ancestor with all its descendants.
A tree is either rooted or unrooted. In a rooted tree the root marks the oldest ancestor, so the order of events can be read off. Distance methods give unrooted trees, and a root is added either with an outgroup, a sequence known to have branched off first, or, as here, at the midpoint of the longest path.

The notebook uses these ideas to build a tree of α-globin, β-globin and myoglobin from human, mouse and chicken:






Figure 4.5: A gene tree of nine globins (neighbour joining on the fraction of differing residues in pairwise BLOSUM62 alignments, midpoint-rooted). Red squares: gene duplications, where both branches contain the same species; the copies below them are paralogs. Blue circles: speciations; the copies are orthologs.



This tree is a gene tree, and comparing it with the species tree (in which chicken branched off before human and mouse) tells the two kinds of homolog apart. The first split separates myoglobin from the haemoglobins, and the second separates α- from β-globin. Both splits are duplications, because each branch still contains all three species, so the genes must have been copied before birds and mammals diverged. Every node below them follows the species tree, with human and mouse joining first, so those nodes are speciations. Human and mouse α-globin are therefore orthologs (human α-globin differs from mouse α-globin at 14% of positions, and from chicken α-globin at 30%), while human α- and β-globin are paralogs (54% different).
Two cautions apply. First, a tree does not by itself say how much each branch can be trusted. This is usually measured by bootstrap support: the alignment columns are resampled many times, the tree is rebuilt each time, and we count how often each branch reappears. Second, real phylogenetics uses models of how residues substitute, together with maximum likelihood (for example IQ-TREE or FastTree), whereas this course only needs the concepts. The fact that sequences are related by a tree comes back in Session 8’s homology-aware splits and in Session 12’s coevolution.

4.9.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Phylogenetic tree, Neighbor joining and UPGMA
Saitou & Nei (1987), The neighbor-joining method: a new method for reconstructing phylogenetic trees, Mol Biol Evol 4:406-425

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
section: 4.10 Reading an alignment: entropy and sequence logos
text:
4.10 Reading an alignment: entropy and sequence logos
A multiple alignment of a whole family is too large to read row by row, so we need a way to summarise it. What matters is how each column varies. A position where every sequence has the same residue has been conserved through evolution, usually because it matters for structure or function. A position with many different residues, in contrast, is free to change.
Session 1’s entropy puts a number on this variation. For the residue frequencies \(p_a\) in a column, the entropy is
\[
H = -\sum_a p_a \log_2 p_a
\]
It is 0 bits for a fully conserved column and at most \(\log_2 20 \approx 4.32\) bits for a protein column where all 20 amino acids are equally common (\(\log_2 4 = 2\) bits for DNA). The column’s information content is the distance from that maximum, \(\log_2 20 - H\), so it is high for conserved columns and near zero for variable ones. (This is the simple version, which assumes that all amino acids are equally common in the background. Logo programs often correct for background frequencies and for small samples.)
A sequence logo (Schneider & Stephens 1990) turns these numbers into a picture by drawing each column as a stack of letters. The height of the stack is the column’s information content, and the height of each letter within the stack is its frequency. A tall stack with one big letter is therefore a conserved position, and a low stack of many small letters is a variable one. In the logo below, gaps also lower the stack, because the height is multiplied by the fraction of sequences that have a residue in that column.
The logo of the Pfam globin family, 73 globins from bacteria, plants, worms, insects and vertebrates, shows how few positions are conserved across the whole family:






Figure 4.6: Sequence logo of the Pfam Globin (PF00042) seed alignment: 73 sequences, 141 columns. Stack height is the information content in bits; letter height is the residue’s frequency. Colours by chemistry: hydrophobic black, polar green, basic blue, acidic red, amide purple. The three labelled columns are numbered as in human beta-globin (HBB, mature chain).



Only two columns are identical in all 73 sequences. One is His92 (F8, the “proximal” histidine, whose side chain binds the haem iron), and the other is Phe42 (CD1, which packs against the haem). A third, His63 (E7, the “distal” histidine, on the oxygen-binding side of the haem), is His in 73% of the sequences. The average column carries only 1.2 bits. The rest of the fold is held together by positions that stay hydrophobic (the black L, V, I and F stacks, often with several residues sharing a column) rather than by identical residues. An alignment can therefore point to the residues a protein cannot do without. It also shows how the same globin fold is kept even though most pairs of sequences in this alignment share fewer than 20% of their residues.
A motif without a family: signal peptides. Logos are not only for families of homologs. Many proteins that are secreted, or that end up in a membrane or in an organelle of the secretory pathway, begin with a signal peptide. This short N-terminal sequence, typically 15-30 residues long, sends the new chain into the secretory pathway, and it is cut off once it has done its job. The signal peptides of unrelated proteins share no ancestor and cannot be aligned residue by residue, but they share a design. The first collections, of a few dozen sequences around 1980, already showed a positively charged N-terminus, then a hydrophobic stretch, then a more polar end. The three parts are now called the n-region, the h-region and the c-region. We can draw the design as a logo if we line the signal peptides up on the one position they all have, the cleavage site, instead of aligning them by homology:






Figure 4.7: Sequence logos of experimentally supported signal peptides from UniProt (the Session 11 dataset), aligned on the cleavage site (dashed line). Positions −25 to −1 are the end of the signal peptide, +1 to +3 the start of the mature protein. Letters are coloured by property: hydrophobic dark grey, small (A, G, S) green, positive blue, negative red, other polar purple. The two logos have different y-scales.



The logo shows two kinds of signal. In the h-region no column is conserved, but every column leans the same way, towards hydrophobic residues and above all leucine. What matters there is a property of a whole stretch, not a residue at a given position. Near the cut, in contrast, two single positions stand out. Positions −3 and −1 carry small, uncharged residues (mostly alanine, also glycine and serine), while position −2, between them, is free. This is the (−3, −1) rule, found in 1983 in a collection of 78 signal peptides (von Heijne, Eur. J. Biochem. 133:17). The enzyme that cuts, signal peptidase, needs small side chains at these two positions. The positively charged n-region is blurred in the logo, because signal peptides differ in length, so the left-hand columns mix residues from different regions. It is clearest in bacteria (K and R).
Like a family’s logo, this description can be turned into a score (Session 5’s PSSM). In 1986, von Heijne built a position weight matrix for positions −13 to +2 around the cleavage site (Nucleic Acids Res. 14:4683). The signal peptide comes back several times in the course. Session 7 compares this weight matrix with a neural network, Session 8 uses the hydrophobicity of the h-region as a feature, and Session 11 lets recurrent networks find the regions by themselves.
Two practical notes apply to logos. With few sequences, the frequencies are noisy and a column can look conserved by chance, so logo programs often apply a small-sample correction. Closely related sequences are also over-represented in most alignments, so real tools weight the sequences as well.
A multiple alignment is therefore more than a picture, because each column gives a distribution of amino acids. Session 5 turns these distributions into position-specific scores.

4.10.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Multiple sequence alignment — additional methods and applications, e.g. profile HMMs, which Session 5 picks up in full
von Heijne (1990), The signal peptide, J. Membr. Biol. 115:195, a short review of the signal-peptide design
Wikipedia, Sequence logo; Schneider & Stephens (1990), “Sequence logos: a new way to display consensus sequences,” Nucleic Acids Research 18:6097-6100

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.11 The course notebook
notebooks/session04-alignment-in-code.ipynb implements Needleman-Wunsch and Smith-Waterman from scratch, adapted from Lukas Käll’s open-access bibook (CC BY 4.0). It starts with amino-acid sequences and a simple identity scoring scheme, in which a match scores +1 and any mismatch or gap −1. This is the \(V(i,j)\) recurrence above, with the identity matrix standing in for \(s(x_i, y_j)\).
Rather than presenting a finished matrix, the notebook fills a small worked example one cell at a time, with the reasoning printed out. The example is a real HBB fragment aligned against a hypothetical mutated variant of it. You then complete a partially filled matrix yourself before the real one is revealed, and the traceback is walked through in the same step-by-step way. Both halves of the algorithm thus appear as a sequence of small decisions rather than as a finished picture.
The notebook then replaces the flat identity scheme with a real substitution matrix, the PAM250 matrix from the “Substitution matrices” section above, loaded from Biopython rather than typed in by hand. With it, the notebook compares global and local alignment of two real globin fragments (from HBB and myoglobin) that share one conserved motif but differ elsewhere. This makes two things directly visible: the practical difference between the two algorithms, and the effect of a graded substitution matrix compared with a flat identity scheme. Finally, the notebook builds the globin gene tree of the section “From alignment to tree” by neighbour joining. Open it in Google Colab via the badge at the top of the notebook page to edit and run it yourself.

title: 4  Session 4: Sequence Alignment
text:
4.14 What’s next
Sequence alignment infers which residues correspond from the sequences alone, and Session 6 asks the same question directly in 3D, with structure alignment. Before that, Session 5 takes up two problems that this session leaves open. First, exact dynamic programming such as Needleman-Wunsch does not scale to searching a new sequence against an entire database, and that is what BLAST’s heuristic is for. Second, once we have many aligned sequences rather than two, we can build a profile from them.

title: Session 4 — Sequence Alignment in code
Session 4 — Sequence Alignment in code
text:
A small worked example, step by step
VHLT is a real 4-residue fragment of human beta-globin (HBB, positions 2-5 — the same protein used as the running example on Sessions 3 and 5). VLC is a hypothetical mutated variant of it, 3 residues long, with the H deleted and the final T substituted by C — small enough to fill in completely by hand, and rigged to need all three kinds of move (a match, a gap, and a mismatch), just like the Session 4 page’s own worked example.
Rather than jumping straight to the finished matrix, the cell below fills it in one cell at a time, printing the three candidate scores (diagonal match/mismatch, up gap, left gap) and which one won, as the recurrence
\[
V(i,j) = \max \begin{cases} V(i-1,j-1) + s(x_i, y_j) \\ V(i-1,j) + g \\ V(i,j-1) + g \end{cases}
\]
is applied in practice.

seqA, seqB = "VHLT", "VLC"
match, mismatch, gap = 1.0, -1.0, -1.0

def score(a, b):
    if a == '-' or b == '-':
        return gap
    return match if a == b else mismatch

m, n = len(seqA) + 1, len(seqB) + 1
S = np.full((m, n), np.nan)
trace = np.zeros((m, n, 2))

print(f"Aligning seqA = {seqA!r} against seqB = {seqB!r}")
print(f"match = {match}, mismatch = {mismatch}, gap = {gap}")
print()

S[0, 0] = 0.0
print("S[0,0] = 0   (both sequences empty)")
for i in range(1, m):
    S[i, 0] = i * gap
    trace[i, 0, :] = (-1, 0)
    print(f"S[{i},0] = {i} x gap = {S[i,0]:.0f}   ({seqA[:i]!r} vs nothing: {i} gap(s))")
for j in range(1, n):
    S[0, j] = j * gap
    trace[0, j, :] = (0, -1)
    print(f"S[0,{j}] = {j} x gap = {S[0,j]:.0f}   (nothing vs {seqB[:j]!r}: {j} gap(s))")

print()
print("Border filled in. So far:")
print(S)
print()
print("Now the interior, one cell at a time:")
print()

for i in range(1, m):
    for j in range(1, n):
        diag = S[i-1, j-1] + score(seqA[i-1], seqB[j-1])
        up = S[i-1, j] + gap
        left = S[i, j-1] + gap
        best = max(diag, up, left)
        S[i, j] = best
        if diag >= max(up, left):
            trace[i, j, :] = (-1, -1)
            move = "diagonal"
        elif up >= left:
            trace[i, j, :] = (-1, 0)
            move = "up"
        else:
            trace[i, j, :] = (0, -1)
            move = "left"
        kind = "match" if seqA[i-1] == seqB[j-1] else "mismatch"
        print(f"S[{i},{j}]: {seqA[i-1]} vs {seqB[j-1]} ({kind}) "
              f"-> diag={diag:.0f}, up={up:.0f}, left={left:.0f}  =>  max = {best:.0f}  ({move})")
    print(f"  -- row {i} complete: {S[i]}")
    print()

print("Completed matrix:")
print(S)

Real substitution matrices: PAM250
Every alignment so far used a flat identity scheme: any matching pair of residues scores \(+1\), any mismatching pair scores \(-1\), no matter which residues they are. Real alignment tools don’t do this — they use substitution matrices like the PAM and BLOSUM families introduced earlier on the Session 4 page, built from real observed substitution frequencies, because not every substitution is equally likely or equally disruptive: swapping a leucine for a similar isoleucine happens all the time and barely changes a protein’s structure, while swapping it for a proline (which breaks helices) is rare and consequential.
Below is the real PAM250 matrix (Dayhoff, Schwartz & Orcutt, 1978), loaded from Biopython rather than typed in by hand, compared directly against the flat identity scheme used so far:

from Bio.Align import substitution_matrices

pam250 = substitution_matrices.load("PAM250")

print(f"{'pair':6}{'identity':>10}{'PAM250':>10}")
for a, b in [("L", "L"), ("L", "I"), ("L", "P"), ("W", "W"), ("W", "Y"), ("W", "D"), ("K", "R"), ("K", "D")]:
    ident = 1.0 if a == b else -1.0
    print(f"{a}-{b:<4}{ident:>+10.0f}{pam250[a, b]:>+10.0f}")

pair    identity    PAM250
L-L           +1        +6
L-I           -1        +2
L-P           -1        -3
W-W           +1       +17
W-Y           -1        +0
W-D           -1        -7
K-R           -1        +3
K-D           -1        +0


Two things to notice: PAM250 still rewards an exact match more than any substitution (L-L scores \(+6\), higher than any L-X substitution), but unlike the flat scheme, not every mismatch costs the same. L-I (both branched hydrophobic residues) scores \(+2\) — better than the flat \(-1\), because that substitution is biologically mild and evolutionarily common. L-P scores \(-3\) — worse than the flat \(-1\), because proline’s rigid ring breaks the local structure a leucine would normally support. Same story for K-R (+3, both positively charged) versus W-D (-7, about as different as two residues get).
This graded scoring is why real tools use PAM/BLOSUM instead of a flat penalty. The small-example traceback walkthrough right after this keeps using the identity scheme, so the arithmetic stays easy to follow by hand — but the final Needleman-Wunsch/Smith-Waterman example further below switches to this real PAM250 matrix instead, by generalizing global_align and local_align (defined above) to accept an optional substitution matrix in place of match/mismatch.


Tracing back, step by step
Filling the matrix only gives the best score — the alignment itself comes from tracing back through the choices that were made along the way, starting at the bottom-right corner (for a global alignment) and following each cell’s winning move back to the top-left. The function below walks that path one step at a time, re-showing the same three candidates that were computed while filling the matrix, so it’s clear why each step goes the direction it does — building the aligned strings up from the end backwards, rather than presenting them ready-made.

def verbose_traceback(seqA, seqB, S, trace, gap, match=1.0, mismatch=-1.0, subst_matrix=None, global_alignment=True):
    """Walk the traceback path one step at a time, printing which move was taken and why."""
    def score(a, b):
        if a == '-' or b == '-':
            return gap
        if subst_matrix is not None:
            return subst_matrix[a, b]
        return match if a == b else mismatch

    if global_alignment:
        i, j = len(seqA), len(seqB)
        def still_going(i, j):
            return i > 0 or j > 0
    else:
        i, j = np.unravel_index(S.argmax(), S.shape)
        def still_going(i, j):
            return min(trace[i, j]) < 0

    outA, outB = "", ""
    step = 1
    print(f"Starting at S[{i},{j}] = {S[i,j]:.0f}")
    print()
    while still_going(i, j):
        di, dj = trace[i, j]
        diag = S[i-1, j-1] + score(seqA[i-1], seqB[j-1]) if i > 0 and j > 0 else -np.inf
        up = S[i-1, j] + gap if i > 0 else -np.inf
        left = S[i, j-1] + gap if j > 0 else -np.inf
        if di == -1 and dj == -1:
            move, resA, resB = "diagonal", seqA[i-1], seqB[j-1]
        elif di == -1 and dj == 0:
            move, resA, resB = "up (gap in seqB)", seqA[i-1], "-"
        else:
            move, resA, resB = "left (gap in seqA)", "-", seqB[j-1]
        print(f"Step {step}: at S[{i},{j}]  (diag={diag:.0f}, up={up:.0f}, left={left:.0f})"
              f"  ->  took {move}: align {resA!r} / {resB!r}")
        outA = resA + outA
        outB = resB + outB
        i, j = i + int(di), j + int(dj)
        step += 1

    print()
    print(f"Reached S[{i},{j}] = {S[i,j]:.0f}"
          f"  -- {'the start of both sequences' if global_alignment else 'a zero'}, traceback complete.")
    print()
    print("Alignment built up step by step:")
    print(outA)
    print(outB)
    return outA, outB


_ = verbose_traceback(seqA, seqB, S, trace, gap, match, mismatch, global_alignment=True)

Step 3: at S[2,1]  (diag=-2, up=0, left=-3)  ->  took up (gap in seqB): align 'H' / '-'

Visualizing the matrix and the traceback path

def plot_dp_matrix(seqA, seqB, S, trace, title, global_alignment=True):
    m, n = S.shape
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(1.1*n + 1, 1.1*m + 1))
    ax.imshow(S, cmap="Blues", alpha=0.6)

    for i in range(m):
        for j in range(n):
            ax.text(j, i, f"{S[i,j]:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11)

    # highlight the traceback path
    if global_alignment:
        i, j = m - 1, n - 1
    else:
        i, j = np.unravel_index(S.argmax(), S.shape)
    path = [(i, j)]
    while (global_alignment and (i > 0 or j > 0)) or (not global_alignment and min(trace[i, j]) < 0):
        di, dj = trace[i, j]
        if di == 0 and dj == 0:
            break
        i, j = i + int(di), j + int(dj)
        path.append((i, j))
    for (pi, pj) in path:
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((pj-0.5, pi-0.5), 1, 1, fill=False, edgecolor="crimson", linewidth=2.5))

    ax.set_xticks(range(n)); ax.set_xticklabels(list("-" + seqB))
    ax.set_yticks(range(m)); ax.set_yticklabels(list("-" + seqA))
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.xaxis.tick_top()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

plot_dp_matrix(seqA, seqB, S, trace, "Needleman-Wunsch: VHLT vs VLC (global)")

title: Session 4 — Sequence Alignment in code
text:
Smith-Waterman (local alignment)

def local_align(seqA, seqB, match=1.0, mismatch=-1.0, gap=-1.0, subst_matrix=None):
    def score(a, b):
        if a == '-' or b == '-':
            return gap
        if subst_matrix is not None:
            return subst_matrix[a, b]
        return match if a == b else mismatch

    m, n = len(seqA) + 1, len(seqB) + 1
    S = np.zeros((m, n))
    trace = np.zeros((m, n, 2))

    for i in range(1, m):
        for j in range(1, n):
            diag = S[i-1, j-1] + score(seqA[i-1], seqB[j-1])
            up = S[i-1, j] + gap
            left = S[i, j-1] + gap
            S[i, j] = max(diag, up, left, 0.0)
            if S[i, j] == 0:
                trace[i, j, :] = (0, 0)
            elif diag >= max(up, left):
                trace[i, j, :] = (-1, -1)
            elif up >= left:
                trace[i, j, :] = (-1, 0)
            else:
                trace[i, j, :] = (0, -1)
    return S, trace


Global vs. local, side by side
Two real 11-residue fragments that share one strong conserved region but differ everywhere else: SAVTALWGKVN from human beta-globin (HBB) and QLVLNVWGKVE from human myoglobin (MYG) — two paralogous globins (see Session 3/5) whose sequences have diverged overall but still share the WGKV motif that is part of the conserved globin fold. Global alignment is forced to account for the mismatched residues on both sides of that motif too, while local alignment finds just the strong match in the middle.
This time, instead of the flat identity scheme, both alignments below are scored with the real PAM250 matrix introduced above — with a correspondingly larger gap penalty (\(-8\) rather than \(-1\)), since PAM250’s match scores range far higher (up to \(+17\) for W-W) than the flat \(+1\) used before; a gap penalty still stuck at the old scale would make gaps effectively free.

seqA, seqB = "SAVTALWGKVN", "QLVLNVWGKVE"
pam_gap = -8.0

S_g, trace_g = global_align(seqA, seqB, gap=pam_gap, subst_matrix=pam250)
outA_g, outB_g = format_alignment(seqA, seqB, S_g, trace_g)
print("Global (Needleman-Wunsch), scored with PAM250:")
print(outA_g)
print(outB_g)
print("Score:", S_g[-1, -1])
print()

S_l, trace_l = local_align(seqA, seqB, gap=pam_gap, subst_matrix=pam250)
outA_l, outB_l = format_local_alignment(seqA, seqB, S_l, trace_l)
print("Local (Smith-Waterman), scored with PAM250:")
print(outA_l)
print(outB_l)
print("Score:", S_l.max())

Tracing back both alignments, step by step
The same verbose_traceback helper works for both — for the local alignment it starts at the single highest-scoring cell instead of the bottom-right corner, and stops as soon as it reaches a zero instead of the top-left. Both calls below pass subst_matrix=pam250, so the diagonal/up/left candidates printed at each step are the real PAM250-scored ones, not the flat identity scheme used earlier.

print("Global traceback:")
print()
_ = verbose_traceback(seqA, seqB, S_g, trace_g, pam_gap, subst_matrix=pam250, global_alignment=True)

print()
print("=" * 60)

plot_dp_matrix(seqA, seqB, S_l, trace_l, "Smith-Waterman (local)", global_alignment=False)















Notice how the local alignment’s matrix has no negative numbers (any candidate score below zero is reset to zero, per Smith-Waterman’s rule), and its traceback path is short — it starts at the single highest-scoring cell and stops as soon as it hits a zero, rather than being forced all the way to a corner. That’s the mechanical difference described on the Session 4 page, now visible directly in the matrix.
Also notice that with PAM250, the local alignment’s matched core is longer than just the WGKV motif found earlier under the flat identity scheme — it extends to include neighbouring positions like L-V (\(+2\), a mild hydrophobic substitution) and T-L (\(-2\), mildly unfavourable but not disqualifying) that a flat \(-1\) mismatch penalty would have made too costly to keep. A real substitution matrix lets the alignment “see” that some substitutions are almost free biologically, so the true similarity block can extend further than strict identity scoring would allow.

Try it yourself
Change seqA/seqB above to your own sequences, or change the match/mismatch/gap scores, and re-run — in particular, try making the gap penalty very large or very small and see how that changes which alignment wins. You can also swap pam250 for another real matrix from Biopython’s collection, e.g. substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62"), and see how the alignment and its score change.

title: Session 4 — Sequence Alignment in code
text:
From alignment to tree
A multiple alignment says which residues correspond; a phylogenetic tree proposes how the sequences are related by descent. The quickest way from one to the other uses the same ingredient as a guide tree: a matrix of pairwise distances. Here: α-globin, β-globin and myoglobin from human, mouse and chicken. The distance between two proteins is the fraction of aligned residues that differ, and neighbour joining builds the tree. A node where the two branches contain the same species is a gene duplication: the copies below it are paralogs. A node that splits species is a speciation: the copies are orthologs.

import io
from Bio import SeqIO, Phylo
from Bio.Align import PairwiseAligner, substitution_matrices
from Bio.Phylo.TreeConstruction import DistanceMatrix, DistanceTreeConstructor
from Bio.Phylo.BaseTree import Clade
import os
FIGS = "../figs" if os.path.isdir("../figs") else "."

# alpha-globin, beta-globin and myoglobin from human, mouse and chicken (UniProt
# P69905, P68871, P02144, P01942, P02088, P04247, P01994, P02112, P02197)
GLOBINS = """
>HBA_human
MVLSPADKTNVKAAWGKVGAHAGEYGAEALERMFLSFPTTKTYFPHFDLSHGSAQVKGHGKKVADALTNAVAHVDDMPNALSALSDLHAHKLRVDPVNFKLLSHCLLVTLAAHLPAEFTPAVHASLDKFLASVSTVLTSKYR
>HBB_human
MVHLTPEEKSAVTALWGKVNVDEVGGEALGRLLVVYPWTQRFFESFGDLSTPDAVMGNPKVKAHGKKVLGAFSDGLAHLDNLKGTFATLSELHCDKLHVDPENFRLLGNVLVCVLAHHFGKEFTPPVQAAYQKVVAGVANALAHKYH
>MB_human
MGLSDGEWQLVLNVWGKVEADIPGHGQEVLIRLFKGHPETLEKFDKFKHLKSEDEMKASEDLKKHGATVLTALGGILKKKGHHEAEIKPLAQSHATKHKIPVKYLEFISECIIQVLQSKHPGDFGADAQGAMNKALELFRKDMASNYKELGFQG
>HBA_mouse
MVLSGEDKSNIKAAWGKIGGHGAEYGAEALERMFASFPTTKTYFPHFDVSHGSAQVKGHGKKVADALASAAGHLDDLPGALSALSDLHAHKLRVDPVNFKLLSHCLLVTLASHHPADFTPAVHASLDKFLASVSTVLTSKYR
>HBB_mouse
MVHLTDAEKAAVSCLWGKVNSDEVGGEALGRLLVVYPWTQRYFDSFGDLSSASAIMGNAKVKAHGKKVITAFNDGLNHLDSLKGTFASLSELHCDKLHVDPENFRLLGNMIVIVLGHHLGKDFTPAAQAAFQKVVAGVATALAHKYH
>MB_mouse
MGLSDGEWQLVLNVWGKVEADLAGHGQEVLIGLFKTHPETLDKFDKFKNLKSEEDMKGSEDLKKHGCTVLTALGTILKKKGQHAAEIQPLAQSHATKHKIPVKYLEFISEIIIEVLKKRHSGDFGADAQGAMSKALELFRNDIAAKYKELGFQG
>HBA_chicken
MVLSAADKNNVKGIFTKIAGHAEEYGAETLERMFTTYPPTKTYFPHFDLSHGSAQIKGHGKKVVAALIEAANHIDDIAGTLSKLSDLHAHKLRVDPVNFKLLGQCFLVVVAIHHPAALTPEVHASLDKFLCAVGTVLTAKYR
>HBB_chicken
MVHWTAEEKQLITGLWGKVNVAECGAEALARLLIVYPWTQRFFASFGNLSSPTAILGNPMVRAHGKKVLTSFGDAVKNLDNIKNTFSQLSELHCDKLHVDPENFRLLGDILIIVLAAHFSKDFTPECQAAWQKLVRVVAHALARKYH
>MB_chicken
MGLSDQEWQQVLTIWGKVEADIAGHGHEVLMRLFHDHPETLDRFDKFKGLKTPDQMKGSEDLKKHGATVLTQLGKILKQKGNHESELKPLAQTHATKHKIPVKYLEFISEVIIKVIAEKHAADFGADSQAAMKKALELFRNDMASKYKEFGFQG
"""
records = list(SeqIO.parse(io.StringIO(GLOBINS.strip()), "fasta"))
names = [r.id.replace("_", " ") for r in records]
aligner = PairwiseAligner(mode="global", substitution_matrix=substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62"),
                          open_gap_score=-10, extend_gap_score=-0.5)

def p_distance(a, b):
    """Fraction of aligned (non-gap) positions that differ, from the best global alignment."""
    aln = aligner.align(a, b)[0]
    pairs = [(x, y) for x, y in zip(aln[0], aln[1]) if x != "-" and y != "-"]
    return sum(x != y for x, y in pairs) / len(pairs)

n = len(records)
D = np.zeros((n, n))
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i):
        D[i, j] = D[j, i] = p_distance(str(records[i].seq), str(records[j].seq))
print("distance (fraction of differing aligned residues), a few pairs:")
for a, b in [("HBA human", "HBA mouse"), ("HBA human", "HBA chicken"), ("HBA human", "HBB human"), ("HBA human", "MB human")]:
    print(f"  {a:12s} vs {b:12s} {D[names.index(a), names.index(b)]:.2f}")

dm = DistanceMatrix(names, [list(D[i, :i + 1]) for i in range(n)])
tree = DistanceTreeConstructor().nj(dm)
tree.root_at_midpoint()             # root halfway along the longest path: here between myoglobin and haemoglobin
tree.ladderize()

def species(clade):
    return {t.name.split()[1] for t in clade.get_terminals()}
dup, spec = [], []
for clade in tree.get_nonterminals():
    kids = clade.clades
    if len(kids) == 2:
        (dup if species(kids[0]) & species(kids[1]) else spec).append(clade)
print(f"\n{len(dup)} duplication nodes, {len(spec)} speciation nodes")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
Phylo.draw(tree, axes=ax, do_show=False, label_func=lambda c: c.name if c.is_terminal() else "")
xs = tree.depths(); ys = {}
terms = tree.get_terminals()
for k, t in enumerate(terms): ys[t] = k + 1
def ypos(c):
    if c in ys: return ys[c]
    ys[c] = np.mean([ypos(k) for k in c.clades]); return ys[c]
for c in dup: ax.plot(xs[c], ypos(c), "s", color="#c53030", ms=11, zorder=5)
for c in spec: ax.plot(xs[c], ypos(c), "o", color="#2b6cb0", ms=9, zorder=5)
ax.plot([], [], "s", color="#c53030", label="duplication: the copies are paralogs")
ax.plot([], [], "o", color="#2b6cb0", label="speciation: the copies are orthologs")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=9, frameon=True)
ax.set_xlabel("branch length (fraction of differing residues)"); ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.set_title("Gene tree of nine globins (neighbour joining, midpoint-rooted)", fontsize=11)
for s in ["top", "right", "left"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_yticks([])
plt.savefig(f"{FIGS}/session04-globin-tree.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

distance (fraction of differing aligned residues), a few pairs:
  HBA human    vs HBA mouse    0.14
  HBA human    vs HBA chicken  0.30
  HBA human    vs HBB human    0.54
  HBA human    vs MB human     0.71

2 duplication nodes, 6 speciation nodes









Read the tree from the root. The first split separates myoglobin from the haemoglobins: a gene duplication, long before the split between birds and mammals, since all three species have both genes. The second duplication separates α- from β-globin, again before the species split. Within each gene, the tree follows the species: human and mouse (both mammals) are closer to each other than to chicken. So human α-globin and mouse α-globin are orthologs; human α-globin and human β-globin are paralogs, and so are human α-globin and mouse β-globin, although they come from different species.
Two cautions. The root here is placed at the midpoint of the longest path, a guess; real analyses root a tree with an outgroup, a sequence known to have branched off first. And the distances are simple fractions of differing residues; real phylogenetics uses models of how residues substitute, and maximum likelihood (IQ-TREE, FastTree, RAxML).

title: 5  Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods
section: 5.2 The scaling problem, and BLAST’s heuristic answer
text:
5.2 The scaling problem, and BLAST’s heuristic answer
Session 4’s dynamic programming finds the provably optimal alignment between two sequences, but its cost is proportional to the product of their lengths. For two sequences a few hundred residues long, this is no problem. For searching one query against a database, it is. GenBank and UniProt hold well over a hundred million sequences between them, and running full dynamic programming against every entry would take far too long to be useful. A database search therefore needs a faster method.
BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) is such a method, and it trades the guarantee of optimality for speed. Instead of filling a DP matrix for every database sequence, it first looks for short exact or near-exact matches. Only the promising regions that these matches point to get the expensive alignment step. Concretely, BLAST runs in three stages:

Seeding. Break the query into short “words”, list every word that scores well against each of them, and scan the database for occurrences of those words.
Extension. Grow each seed hit outwards, in both directions, into a full local alignment.
Evaluation. Ask whether the score of the resulting alignment is better than what pure chance would produce.

Each stage is covered in its own section below. This three-stage picture is the core idea, and it is deliberately simplified. Production BLAST adds refinements such as the two-hit rule (only extend when two seeds lie close together on the same diagonal), masking of low-complexity regions, gapped extension, and corrections for unusual amino-acid composition. None of these refinements changes the logic of seed, extend, evaluate.

section: 5.3 Stage 1: seeding — turning the query into fast lookups
text:
5.3 Stage 1: seeding — turning the query into fast lookups
The first stage turns the query into a set of short words. For protein sequences, a “word” is usually only 3 residues long, so a query of length 200 has 198 overlapping 3-letter words. BLAST does not search the database only for exact matches to these words, because a biologically real match may substitute a residue or two without losing significance. Instead, it uses a substitution matrix (BLOSUM62, from Session 4) to precompute every 3-letter combination that scores above a threshold \(T\) against each query word.
Worked example. Scored with the real BLOSUM62 matrix, several other words besides the query word LWG itself clear a typical threshold of \(T=12\). The notebook computes them directly from BLOSUM62, and 49 words clear the threshold in total. The top ones are:

These query words and their high-scoring neighbours go into a lookup table, which is built once per query and records, for every 3-letter word, which query positions it would seed. BLAST then scans each database sequence once, from start to end. For every 3-letter word it reads, it asks the table “does this word seed anything in the query, and where?” Because that check is a single table lookup, the scan is fast and linear in the size of the database. Only the few places that produce a seed go on to the expensive extension step.

title: 5  Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods
section: 5.4 Stage 2: extension — growing a seed into a real alignment
text:
5.4 Stage 2: extension — growing a seed into a real alignment
A seed hit is only a 3-letter coincidence and not yet evidence of anything. BLAST therefore extends it outwards in both directions and recomputes a running score as it goes. The scoring uses the same substitution-matrix logic as Session 4’s dynamic programming, but without filling a full matrix. Instead, extension stops as soon as the running score has fallen too far below its own best point so far.
The X-drop rule. BLAST tracks the running score as the alignment extends, and separately the best score seen so far. If the running score ever falls more than a threshold \(X\) below that best score, the alignment is very unlikely to recover, so extension stops. The reported alignment is then trimmed back to the point where the best score occurred.
Worked example, adapted from Korf, Yandell & Bedell (2003). We treat two short strings as if they were sequences, score \(+1\) for a matching character and \(-1\) for a mismatch (ignoring spaces), and use \(X=5\):
query:    Thequickbrownfoxjumps...
database: Thequietbrownncatpurrs...
The running score climbs steadily through Thequ, dips slightly at the ick/iet mismatch, and then recovers and climbs further through brown to a peak of 9 right after ...brown/...brown. After that it falls steadily, as foxjump diverges from catpurr. Once the running score has dropped 5 points below the peak of 9, extension stops. The reported alignment is trimmed back to the peak itself, so it pairs Thequickbrown with Thequietbrown and leaves out the lower-scoring tail beyond it. The notebook reproduces this computation in code.

title: 5  Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods
section: 5.5 Stage 3: is this hit significant? E-values and bit scores
text:
5.5 Stage 3: is this hit significant? E-values and bit scores
Extending every seed produces a raw alignment score. A raw score alone, however, does not say whether the alignment is meaningful or simply what we would expect from two random sequences of that length. To decide, we need to know how scores are distributed by chance. Karlin and Altschul proved in 1990 that the scores from aligning a query against random sequence data follow an extreme value (Gumbel) distribution, not a normal distribution, and this result underpins BLAST’s statistics.
From that distribution follows the expected number of alignments that score at least \(S\) purely by chance, the E-value:
\[
E = K m n\, e^{-\lambda S}
\]
Here \(m\) and \(n\) are the lengths of the query and the database, and \(K\) and \(\lambda\) are constants of the particular scoring system (substitution matrix and gap penalties), which real BLAST output reports as “Karlin-Altschul statistics”. This is the simplified textbook form. Real BLAST replaces \(m\) and \(n\) by slightly smaller effective lengths (an alignment cannot start right at the end of a sequence) and adjusts for composition, but the behaviour is the same.
Two consequences of the formula matter. First, a higher score gives an exponentially smaller \(E\). Second, a bigger database (\(n\)) inflates \(E\) for the same alignment, because chance has more opportunities to produce a false hit. An E-value is therefore only meaningful together with the database it was computed against, and the same alignment can be “significant” against a small database but not against all of GenBank.
Raw scores and E-values both depend on the scoring system, which makes them awkward to compare across different searches. The bit score solves this by normalising away the scoring system:
\[
S' = \frac{\lambda S - \ln K}{\ln 2}
\]
Bit scores from completely different searches, even ones that use different substitution matrices, can therefore be compared directly. A bit score is not a significance test on its own, though. There is no universal bit-score cutoff, because whether a given score is surprising still depends on the size of the search space it was found in. For significance, read the E-value.
Reading real output. A real local BLASTP search of HBB (beta-globin, P68871) against its five closest human globin relatives gives the following hits:

The first four are all confident, high-quality hits, with high percent identity, astronomically small E-values and comfortably high bit scores. Myoglobin is the interesting case. It shares the globin fold and a real evolutionary origin with haemoglobin, yet BLAST reports only a weak alignment with an E-value of 63, which taken at face value is no statistical evidence at all. That number, however, only evaluates the alignment BLAST found. If we run the same search with the two-hit rule switched off (so that every single seed gets extended; -window_size 0 in BLAST+), BLAST finds a full-length alignment, 145 residues at 25.5% identity, with an E-value of 5×10⁻¹¹. With the default settings, no pair of seeds happened to fall close enough together on the right diagonal, so the good alignment was never extended. This is the price of a heuristic. BLAST is fast because it skips most of the search, and occasionally it skips the answer, which an optimal Smith–Waterman search would not have missed.
Database size still matters as well. These E-values are relative to a tiny five-sequence database. Against a database the size of UniProtKB (about \(9\times10^{10}\) residues), the same full-length myoglobin alignment would get an E-value of about 0.007, which is significant, but only just. Relatives that have diverged further than myoglobin, such as the bacterial truncated haemoglobins, give no detectable pairwise signal at all, even with the optimal alignment (Session 6 shows that they still share the globin fold).

title: 5  Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods
section: 5.6 BLAST’s ideas at modern database scale: MMseqs2
text:
5.6 BLAST’s ideas at modern database scale: MMseqs2
BLAST was designed in 1990, when the protein databases held tens of thousands of sequences. Today’s metagenomic collections hold billions, and at that scale even BLAST becomes too slow. MMseqs2 (Steinegger & Söding, 2017) is a widely used modern search tool that keeps BLAST’s logic but turns one part of it around. In simplified form, it works as follows:

Index the target database by short words (k-mers, typically 6–7 residues for proteins). The index is a table that maps each k-mer to the database sequences and positions where it occurs, and it is built once and reused.
For each k-mer in the query, generate the similar k-mers (scored with a substitution matrix, exactly like BLAST’s neighbour words) and look them up in the index.
Keep only database sequences in which two matching k-mers fall on the same diagonal, that is, at the same offset between query and target position, just as in a dot plot from Session 4. Two consistent hits are much stronger evidence of a real alignment than one.
Score the surviving candidates quickly with an ungapped alignment along that diagonal, and discard the weak ones.
Run the expensive gapped Smith–Waterman alignment, heavily optimised to use the processor’s vector instructions, only on the small set that is left.

The difference from classic BLAST lies in which side gets indexed. BLAST builds a lookup table from the query and its neighbour words, and then reads through every database sequence. MMseqs2 instead indexes the database once, so each query only has to look up its own k-mers. Steps 3–5 form a cascade of ever more expensive filters, each of which passes on only a small fraction of the candidates. As a result, MMseqs2 is often hundreds of times faster than BLAST at similar sensitivity. No machine learning is involved, because MMseqs2 simply engineers the same seed-extend-evaluate ideas for scale.
Like PSI-BLAST below, MMseqs2 can also iterate, turning its hits into a profile and searching again, and ColabFold uses it to build the alignments that AlphaFold needs (Session 12). Session 6 meets its structural counterpart, Foldseek, from the same group.
