title: 5  Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods
section: 5.7 From one sequence to many: PSI-BLAST and the PSSM
text:
5.7 From one sequence to many: PSI-BLAST and the PSSM
Myoglobin sits near the edge of what a single sequence can detect, and more distant relatives lie beyond it. The reason is that ordinary BLAST scores everything against one fixed substitution matrix, whatever family the query belongs to, so a faint but real family signal is easily lost against the background of a large database. PSI-BLAST (Position-Specific Iterated BLAST) does better, because it builds a query-specific scoring matrix and refines it over several rounds:

Run an ordinary BLAST search with the query sequence.
Take the hits that pass the inclusion threshold (an E-value cutoff, by default stricter than the one used for reporting hits), align them to the query, and turn that alignment into a position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM), described below. Hits that are displayed but fall short of the inclusion threshold do not enter the profile.
Search the database again, this time scoring with the PSSM instead of a generic substitution matrix.
Repeat, so that each round’s included hits refine the PSSM further, until no new sequences pass the threshold (convergence) or a set number of rounds is reached.

This makes PSI-BLAST more sensitive than a single BLAST pass, particularly for remote homologs whose similarity to the original query is too faint for a fixed substitution matrix to catch.
Iteration is not automatically better: profile drift. Suppose that one unrelated sequence passes the inclusion threshold. It then enters the alignment and shifts the next PSSM a little towards itself. The next round finds more sequences like the intruder, which shift the profile further. After a few rounds, the “family” can be dominated by proteins that have nothing to do with the original query, often through a shared low-complexity or coiled-coil region rather than real homology. This is a general lesson that returns in the machine-learning half of the course. A model is only as good as the examples it was built from, and a model that chooses its own training data can reinforce its own mistakes. In practice, keep the inclusion threshold strict, look at what entered in each round, and check surprising late-round hits independently.

5.7.1 Building a PSSM, step by step
Session 4 ended with alignment columns, their entropy, and sequence logos. A logo describes an alignment column, whereas a PSSM turns the same column statistics into numbers that can score a new sequence. The recipe below is a teaching model. The real PSI-BLAST computation also weights the sequences and uses more sophisticated pseudocounts, as noted along the way, but every step serves the same purpose in the real thing.
1. Count. From a multiple sequence alignment, count how often each residue appears at each position. Take this small toy alignment of 5 sequences:
Position:   1 2 3 4 5
Protein 1:  A G L S P
Protein 2:  A G L T P
Protein 3:  R G I S P
Protein 4:  A A L S Q
Protein 5:  A A L S P
At position 1, 4 of the 5 sequences have A and 1 has R. At position 5, 4 have P and 1 has Q, and so on.
Real alignments are rarely this balanced. If a search returns fifty nearly identical mammalian sequences and three distant ones, raw counts would make the profile describe mammals rather than the family. Real tools therefore reduce redundancy or weight sequences, removing or down-weighting near-duplicates so that an over-represented subfamily does not dominate the counts. The exact recipe varies between programs, but the principle is what matters.
2. Add pseudocounts. Turning raw counts straight into frequencies causes two problems. First, a residue that never appears at a position gets a frequency of exactly zero, and its log-odds score becomes \(-\infty\). Second, with only 5 sequences, the absence of a residue might be bad luck rather than a real biological signal. Pseudocounts, small constants added to every count before the frequencies are computed, solve both problems. In our teaching model we add \(+1\) uniformly to the count of every residue type at every position. Conceptually, a pseudocount is a prior, that is, what we assume about a column before looking at the alignment (here, “every residue is possible”). With only five sequences the prior has a large influence, while with hundreds of sequences the observed counts swamp it. Real tools use smarter priors, for example by giving larger pseudocounts to residues that substitute easily for the observed ones (according to a substitution matrix).
3. Compare to background. Compute each residue’s background frequency \(q_j\), that is, how often it occurs in proteins generally (e.g. alanine ≈7.4%, tryptophan ≈1.3%), independently of this alignment.
4. Compute log-odds scores. For each position \(i\) and residue \(j\),
\[
S_{i,j} = \log_2 \frac{f_{i,j}}{q_j}
\]
Here \(f_{i,j}\) is the (pseudocount-adjusted) observed frequency. With base 2, a score of \(+1\) means “twice as likely here as by chance”, \(+3\) means “8× as likely”, and so on. Arranged into a matrix, with one row per alignment position and one column per residue, the scores \(S_{i,j}\) are the PSSM. (Some tools store the matrix the other way round, but the orientation is only a storage convention.) Scoring a candidate sequence against the PSSM means looking up one value per position and summing them. This is the weighted-sum, or dot-product, idea from Session 1, generalised to sequence positions.
The notebook builds this PSSM from the alignment above and confirms that the highest-scoring sequence the matrix can produce is AGLSP, the alignment’s own consensus, as it should be.
Why pseudocounts really matter. With only five sequences, every frequency is a small-sample estimate, and the raw log-odds score takes it at face value. Take a position where 4 of 5 sequences show alanine (background 7.4%) and 1 shows the much rarer tryptophan (1.3%). The raw scores are \(\log_2(0.8/0.074) \approx 3.43\) for alanine and \(\log_2(0.2/0.013) \approx 3.94\) for tryptophan, so a single observation outscores four. Yet one tryptophan in five sequences could easily be chance, and the score treats it as a reliable frequency of 20%. With \(+1\) pseudocounts the frequencies become 5/25 and 2/25, and the scores fall to 1.43 and 2.62. The pseudocounts make every score more cautious, but they do not change the ranking: tryptophan still wins. A pseudocount cannot tell a lucky single observation from a real one; only more sequences can.
Gaps. A PSSM contains only substitution scores, one row per position. To align a new sequence to it, PSI-BLAST therefore uses ordinary gapped alignment, the same dynamic programming as in Session 4, with the PSSM row for position \(i\) taking the place of the substitution-matrix row for query residue \(i\). The gap-open and gap-extension penalties are the ordinary ones, the same at every position.
A PSSM is already a linear model. For an ungapped sequence \(x = x_1 x_2 \dots x_L\), the PSSM score is
\[
S(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{L} w[i, x_i],
\]
where \(w[i, x_i]\) is the matrix entry for residue \(x_i\) at position \(i\). The score is thus one weight looked up per position and added up. Session 7 keeps this weighted-sum idea but learns the weights from labelled examples instead of deriving them from alignment counts.

Wikipedia, PSI-BLAST, Position weight matrix, and Pseudocount

title: 5  Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods
section: 5.8 Profile Hidden Markov Models: what a PSSM still can’t represent
text:
5.8 Profile Hidden Markov Models: what a PSSM still can’t represent
A PSSM gives position-specific substitution scores, but the alignment algorithm handles gaps separately, with the same penalties everywhere. Real families are not like that. A loop between two helices may tolerate insertions of any length, while the core of the domain almost never has one. A profile Hidden Markov Model (profile HMM) therefore integrates position-specific match, insertion and deletion behaviour into one probabilistic model of the family. It uses three kinds of states, arranged in a repeating unit with one unit per alignment position:

Match (M) states represent a conserved position. Each has its own per-residue emission probabilities and plays the same role as one column of a PSSM.
Insert (I) states represent extra residues between conserved positions. The model can emit a residue from them and then loop back to allow more than one.
Delete (D) states represent a skipped conserved position and emit nothing at all.

Special Begin and End states bookend the model. Transitions connect the M/I/D states of consecutive positions (e.g. \(M_i \to
M_{i+1}\), \(M_i \to I_i\), \(M_i \to D_{i+1}\)), and each transition has its own learned probability.
Why “hidden”. For an observed residue in a real sequence, the model never tells you directly whether it came from a Match state or an Insert state. That has to be inferred from the path through the states that best explains the whole sequence, using the emission and transition probabilities together. The states generate what you observe, but they themselves stay hidden.
This is the extra structure that PSSMs lack, and it is why profile HMMs, not PSSMs, are the standard tool behind large-scale protein family databases such as Pfam. A profile HMM trained on a protein family can recognise a new sequence as a member even when it has a genuinely different number of residues in a variable region. The model itself has learned where insertions and deletions are common in that family, which a PSSM with uniform gap penalties can only approximate.






NoteWhat neither a PSSM nor a profile HMM can represent



Both models score a sequence position by position. The score is a sum over columns, so each position contributes independently of the others. Real proteins do not always work that way. When mutations interact, so that the effect of one depends on the residue at another position (epistasis), no profile can capture it. Session 9 shows a protein where this matters (all 160,000 variants at four positions of GB1), and Session 12 shows how pairwise models fitted to an alignment (direct coupling analysis) add those interactions.

title: 5  Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods
section: 5.9 Worked example: a real profile-HMM hit on HBB
text:
5.9 Worked example: a real profile-HMM hit on HBB
The same idea works on a real sequence at production scale. To tie this back to the HBB (beta-globin) locus from Session 3, we search Pfam’s library of profile HMMs against the real UniProt entry P68871 (HBB_HUMAN), fetched live via EBI’s InterPro API. The search finds a match to PF00042 (“Globin”), spanning residues 27-142 of the 147-residue protein, with an E-value of around \(1.3\times10^{-29}\). In a database of this size, essentially no match that good is expected by chance. The profile HMM thus does on a real sequence what the toy PSSM above did on paper: it scores how well a sequence matches a family, position by position.

5.12 The lab
The full lab covers BLAST and profile methods as one continuous exercise. (Session 4 now has its own short lab for alignment practice, so this one no longer needs to cover alignment as well.) You first identify a real, unknown gene from a raw sequence through a real NCBI BLAST search. It turns out to be a sixth real human globin-family gene, continuing this course’s running thread. Three code exercises follow: a real Clustal Omega alignment and PSSM on five globin-family proteins, a real iterated profile search (jackhmmer, the profile-HMM counterpart of PSI-BLAST) that compares its first round with its third against every sequence in the PDB, and a live Pfam domain search for HIV-1’s Gag-Pol polyprotein via the same InterPro API that this page’s HBB worked example uses.
Every search in notebooks/session05-lab.ipynb runs on a server at EMBL-EBI, reached through its web API: the notebook sends the sequences, the server runs the program, and the notebook reads the result back. There is nothing to install, so the lab runs on Colab, in the browser or from VS Code. A remote homolog can become impossible to recognise from its sequence while its fold stays conserved. title: Session 5 — BLAST and Profile Methods in code
text:
Stage 1: seeding — BLOSUM62 neighbor words
For the query word LWG, which other 3-letter words score above a threshold T=12 against it, using the real BLOSUM62 matrix?

from Bio.Align import substitution_matrices
from itertools import product

blosum62 = substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62")
AA = sorted(set(blosum62.alphabet) - {"*", "X", "B", "Z"})

def word_score(w1, w2):
    return sum(blosum62[a, b] for a, b in zip(w1, w2))

query_word = "LWG"
T = 12
scores = {"".join(w): word_score(query_word, "".join(w)) for w in product(AA, repeat=3)}
neighbors = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])
above_threshold = [(w, s) for w, s in neighbors if s >= T]

print(f"{len(above_threshold)} words score >= {T} against {query_word!r}; top 10:")
for w, s in above_threshold[:10]:
    print(f"  {w}  {s}")

title: Session 5 — BLAST and Profile Methods in code
text:
Stage 2: extension — the X-drop rule
Track a running score and a running maximum; stop as soon as the running score falls more than X below the running maximum, then trim back to where that maximum actually occurred.

def xdrop_extend(query, target, X):
    q = query.replace(" ", "")
    t = target.replace(" ", "")
    n = min(len(q), len(t))

    score = 0
    running_max = 0
    max_pos = 0
    trace = []
    for i in range(n):
        score += 1 if q[i] == t[i] else -1
        if score > running_max:
            running_max = score
            max_pos = i
        trace.append(score)
        if running_max - score >= X:
            return {
                "stopped_at": i,
                "peak_score": running_max,
                "peak_position": max_pos,
                "trimmed_query": q[: max_pos + 1],
                "trimmed_target": t[: max_pos + 1],
                "trace": trace,
            }
    return {"stopped_at": None, "peak_score": running_max, "trace": trace}


result = xdrop_extend(
    "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.",
    "The quiet brown cat purrs when she sees him.",
    X=5,
)
print("Extension stopped at character index:", result["stopped_at"])
print("Peak running score:", result["peak_score"], "at position", result["peak_position"])
print("Trimmed alignment:")
print(" query:", result["trimmed_query"])
print(" target:", result["trimmed_target"])
assert result["trimmed_query"] == "Thequickbrown"
assert result["trimmed_target"] == "Thequietbrown"

Peak running score: 9 at position 12
Trimmed alignment:

 target: Thequietbrown

section: Stage 3: a real BLAST search, and what its heuristic missed
text:
Stage 3: a real BLAST search, and what its heuristic missed
The book page’s table comes from a BLASTP search of HBB (beta-globin) against five other human globin-family proteins. It was run with BLAST+, the command-line version of BLAST, when this notebook was written. Its output is reproduced below, so that the notebook needs no command-line tools. The commands are given in a comment for reference.
The sequences themselves are fetched live from UniProt, because the next step aligns two of them again in Python.

import requests

GLOBINS = {
    "P68871": "HBB_HUMAN (beta-globin) -- the query",
    "P69905": "HBA_HUMAN (alpha-globin)",
    "P02144": "MYG_HUMAN (myoglobin)",
    "P02008": "HBAZ_HUMAN (zeta-globin, embryonic alpha-like)",
    "P02042": "HBD_HUMAN (delta-globin)",
    "P02100": "HBE_HUMAN (epsilon-globin, embryonic)",
}

fasta = {}
for acc, label in GLOBINS.items():
    r = requests.get(f"https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/{acc}.fasta", timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    fasta[acc] = r.text
    print(label)

HBB_HUMAN (beta-globin) -- the query
HBA_HUMAN (alpha-globin)
MYG_HUMAN (myoglobin)
HBAZ_HUMAN (zeta-globin, embryonic alpha-like)
HBD_HUMAN (delta-globin)
HBE_HUMAN (epsilon-globin, embryonic)



# Run with BLAST+ 2.16.0, on the five sequences fetched above:
#   makeblastdb -in globin_db.fasta -dbtype prot -out globin_db
#   blastp -query hbb_query.fasta -db globin_db -outfmt "6 sseqid pident length evalue bitscore" -evalue 1000
#   blastp ... -window_size 0 -max_hsps 1        (the same search, with the two-hit rule switched off)
BLAST_DEFAULT = """sp|P02042|HBD_HUMAN  93.197  147 9.28e-105   284
sp|P02100|HBE_HUMAN 75.510  147 2.05e-87    240
sp|P69905|HBA_HUMAN 43.448  145 8.95e-38    114
sp|P02008|HBAZ_HUMAN    35.862  145 3.81e-32    100
sp|P02144|MYG_HUMAN 16.000  125 63  10.8"""
BLAST_NO_TWO_HIT = """sp|P02144|MYG_HUMAN   25.517  145 5.38e-11    45.4"""

def show_blast(table):
    print(f"{'Hit':<20}{'%identity':>10}{'length':>8}{'E-value':>14}{'bit score':>11}")
    for line in table.splitlines():
        sseqid, pident, length, evalue, bitscore = line.split("\t")
        print(f"{sseqid.split('|')[2]:<20}{float(pident):>10.1f}{length:>8}{float(evalue):>14.3g}{float(bitscore):>11.1f}")

show_blast(BLAST_DEFAULT)

Hit                  %identity  length       E-value  bit score
HBD_HUMAN                 93.2     147     9.28e-105      284.0
HBE_HUMAN                 75.5     147      2.05e-87      240.0
HBA_HUMAN                 43.4     145      8.95e-38      114.0
HBAZ_HUMAN                35.9     145      3.81e-32      100.0
MYG_HUMAN                 16.0     125            63       10.8


Four confident hits, and myoglobin with an E-value of about 63. Taken at face value, that is no statistical evidence at all, although myoglobin is a known remote homolog. But an E-value only evaluates the alignment BLAST found. BLAST’s default two-hit rule only extends a seed when a second seed lies nearby on the same diagonal. Is there a better alignment that BLAST never extended? Smith-Waterman (Session 4) finds the best local alignment by full dynamic programming, with no shortcuts. Here it is with BLAST’s own scoring (BLOSUM62, a gap costing 11 to open and 1 per residue):

import math
from Bio import Align
from Bio.Align import substitution_matrices

def seq_of(acc):
    return "".join(fasta[acc].splitlines()[1:])

aligner = Align.PairwiseAligner(mode="local", substitution_matrix=substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62"),
                                open_gap_score=-12, extend_gap_score=-1)   # a gap of length k costs 11 + k, as in BLAST
best = aligner.align(seq_of("P68871"), seq_of("P02144"))[0]
identity = sum(a == b and a != "-" for a, b in zip(best[0], best[1]))
length = best.shape[1]

lam, K = 0.267, 0.041                      # BLAST's Karlin-Altschul parameters for BLOSUM62 with these gap costs
bits = (lam * best.score - math.log(K)) / math.log(2)
m = len(seq_of("P68871"))
n = sum(len(seq_of(acc)) for acc in GLOBINS if acc != "P68871")
E = m * n * 2 ** -bits                     # E-value: the search space times 2 to the minus bit score
print(f"Smith-Waterman, HBB against MYG: raw score {best.score:.0f}, {bits:.1f} bits, "
      f"{length} columns, {100 * identity / length:.1f}% identity, E = {E:.1g}")
print()
print("BLAST with the two-hit rule switched off (-window_size 0) finds the same alignment:")
show_blast(BLAST_NO_TWO_HIT)

Smith-Waterman, HBB against MYG: raw score 110, 47.0 bits, 145 columns, 25.5% identity, E = 8e-10

BLAST with the two-hit rule switched off (-window_size 0) finds the same alignment:
Hit                  %identity  length       E-value  bit score
MYG_HUMAN                 25.5     145      5.38e-11       45.4


The optimal alignment covers almost the whole of both proteins (145 residues, about 25% identity) and is highly significant. BLAST with the two-hit rule switched off finds it too, with almost the same bit score; its E-value is a little smaller because BLAST also corrects for sequence composition and for the ends of the sequences. With the default settings no two seeds happened to land close together on the right diagonal, so the good alignment was never extended: the price of a fast heuristic. More distant relatives than myoglobin give no pairwise signal even with an optimal alignment, which is the case profile methods are built for.

title: Session 5 — BLAST and Profile Methods in code
text:
Building a PSSM from scratch
The same 5-sequence toy alignment from the book page, with and without pseudocounts.

import math

msa = ["AGLSP", "AGLTP", "RGISP", "AALSQ", "AALSP"]

# Typical background frequencies for these residues in proteins
background = {
    "A": 0.074, "R": 0.042, "G": 0.074, "L": 0.076, "S": 0.081,
    "T": 0.062, "P": 0.050, "Q": 0.037, "I": 0.038, "W": 0.013,
}

residues = sorted(r for r in background if r != "W")  # residues that actually appear in this MSA
n_pos = len(msa[0])

def counts_at(pos):
    col = [seq[pos] for seq in msa]
    return {r: col.count(r) for r in residues}

def pssm(pseudocount):
    matrix = []
    for pos in range(n_pos):
        c = counts_at(pos)
        total = sum(c.values()) + pseudocount * len(residues)
        freqs = {r: (c[r] + pseudocount) / total for r in residues}
        matrix.append({r: math.log2(freqs[r] / background[r]) if freqs[r] > 0 else float("-inf") for r in residues})
    return matrix

def best_sequence(matrix):
    best = [max(col, key=col.get) for col in matrix]
    score = sum(matrix[i][best[i]] for i in range(len(best)))
    return "".join(best), score

pssm_pseudo = pssm(pseudocount=1)
best_seq, best_score = best_sequence(pssm_pseudo)
print("With pseudocounts, highest-scoring sequence:", best_seq, f"(score {best_score:.2f})")
assert best_seq == "AGLSP", "should recover the alignment's own consensus"

With pseudocounts, highest-scoring sequence: AGLSP (score 11.43)



# Why pseudocounts matter: a rare residue occurring once can outscore
# a common residue occurring four times, purely because it's rarer overall.
a_count, w_count, n = 4, 1, 5
score_A = math.log2((a_count / n) / background["A"])
score_W = math.log2((w_count / n) / background["W"])
print(f"A (appears in 4/5 sequences):  log-odds = {score_A:.2f}")
print(f"W (appears in 1/5 sequences):  log-odds = {score_W:.2f}")
assert score_W > score_A, "the rare residue should outscore the common one without pseudocounts"

A (appears in 4/5 sequences):  log-odds = 3.43
W (appears in 1/5 sequences):  log-odds = 3.94

title: 6  Session 6: Protein Structure
text:
6.1 Learning goals
By the end of this session you should be able to:
The question for this session is: what information about a protein is contained in its sequence, what becomes visible only in 3D, and how can computers connect the two? Sessions 3–5 worked with sequences, retrieving them, aligning them and searching for families. In Session 3 you also found structures, but only as database records (a PDB entry, an AlphaFold model). In this session the structure itself becomes the data. Its coordinates can be turned into distances, secondary structure, domains and interfaces, and compared with other structures. The course’s globin thread continues as well. In Session 3 you looked up HBB’s identifiers, in Session 4 you aligned globin sequences and in Session 5 you searched for the globin family, and now you compare globin structures.

title: 6  Session 6: Protein Structure
6  Session 6: Protein Structure
text:
6.2 Sequence becomes structure

6.2.1 Four levels, four computational tasks
A protein starts as a polypeptide chain, a linear polymer of amino acids, which folds into a 3D shape. Structural biology describes the result at four levels, and in this course each level comes with its own computational problem:



Table 6.1: The four levels of protein structure and where they appear in the course.











Level
What it is
Computational task
Where in the course




Primary
the amino-acid sequence
alignment, BLAST, profiles
Sessions 3–5


Secondary
local backbone shapes: α-helix, β-strand, coil
prediction from sequence
Sessions 7–11


Tertiary
the 3D fold of one chain
structure comparison, prediction
this session; Session 12


Quaternary
several chains packed together
interfaces, complexes
this session; Session 12







An α-helix is a coil held together by hydrogen bonds between the backbone N-H and C=O groups of residues four apart. A β-sheet is built from extended β-strands that are hydrogen-bonded edge to edge. Everything else is called coil. Programs such as DSSP assign these labels from the coordinates of a solved structure.
The tertiary fold is held together mainly by the hydrophobic effect (non-polar side chains bury themselves away from water), together with hydrogen bonds, electrostatic interactions and van der Waals contacts.
Many proteins work as a single chain, while others assemble into complexes of two to hundreds of chains.



6.2.2 Haemoglobin: all four levels in one protein
Haemoglobin is a heterotetramer of two α-globin chains (141 residues) and two β-globin chains (146 residues; β-globin is HBB, this course’s running example since Session 3). Each chain folds on its own and carries an oxygen-binding haem group. Using PyMOL’s secondary-structure algorithm (dss), the notebook computes that one β chain is 118 of 146 residues (80.8%) α-helix and 0% β-strand. The PDB entry’s own annotation, which Session 7 uses, gives 117 helical residues, because the two methods differ slightly in where exactly a helix ends.






Figure 6.1: PDB entry 2HHB, human deoxyhaemoglobin: two α chains (blue/cyan), two β chains (salmon/pink), four haem iron atoms (orange spheres). Rendered from the real structure with PyMOL.





6.2.3 Does the sequence determine the structure?
Whether a computer can predict a structure at all depends on how much of it the sequence determines. In the 1960s Christian Anfinsen showed that ribonuclease, unfolded in the test tube, refolds into its active shape on its own once the denaturant is removed. For many small globular proteins, then, the sequence contains enough information to specify the native fold under the right conditions, and this principle is what makes structure prediction possible. It is not a law for every protein, however. Some proteins need chaperones to fold efficiently, many need a ligand, cofactor or binding partner, some switch between alternative states (haemoglobin itself, below), and intrinsically disordered regions have no single fold.
Two kinds of interaction build a fold. Local interactions, between residues close in sequence, form secondary structure. The hydrogen bonds of an α-helix, for example, connect residues \(i\) and \(i+4\). Long-range interactions, between residues far apart in sequence but close in space, pack the helices and strands into a tertiary structure. Local structure can therefore be partly guessed from a short window of sequence (Session 7), whereas long-range structure cannot, which is why tertiary-structure prediction is so much harder.


6.2.4 A structure as a matrix: distance and contact maps
A structure file is a list of atomic coordinates, but coordinates are not always the most useful representation. An alternative is the distance between every pair of residues, which for a chain of \(L\) residues gives an \(L \times L\) distance map. Thresholding the distance map gives a contact map, with 1 where two residues are close (here, Cβ atoms within 8 Å) and 0 elsewhere. Unlike coordinates, both maps stay the same however the protein is rotated or moved, so two structures can be compared without first superimposing them.






Figure 6.2: Three representations of β-globin (2HHB, chain B). Left: the 3D structure, coloured from the N-terminus (blue) to the C-terminus (red). Middle: the distance map. Right: the contact map, with the eight α-helices of the PDB file as red bars. The band along the diagonal is each helix in contact with itself (local interactions); the off-diagonal stripes are helices packed against each other (long-range interactions).



This representation returns twice later in the course. First, an \(L
\times L\) map looks like an image, which is why image-processing networks (CNNs, Session 10) turned out to be good at predicting contacts. Second, coevolution, contact prediction and AlphaFold’s “pair representation” (Session 12) all work on residue-pair information like this.






TipRepresentations



The same protein can be represented as a sequence, a profile (Session 5), a set of coordinates, a distance or contact map, or a learned embedding (Session 11). The choice of representation determines which patterns are easy to see and, later in the course, which patterns a model can easily learn.




6.2.5 Looking at structures: PyMOL
To look at a structure yourself, you need a molecular viewer. PyMOL is, with ChimeraX, one of the two most widely used, and its open-source version is free. It loads a structure directly from the PDB and shows it as cartoon (secondary structure as ribbons and arrows, as in the figures above), as sticks (every bond, useful for a side chain or ligand) or as spheres (every atom, useful for packing). It also measures distances and angles directly from the coordinates. This session’s lab uses PyMOL hands-on, but you do not need to install the program: open-source PyMOL is also a Python library, which the lab notebook installs on Colab. You type the same commands as in PyMOL’s own command line, and the notebook draws the picture. The course notebook drives PyMOL the same way, so that its figures and measurements are reproducible.


6.2.6 Further reading

Wikipedia, Protein structure and Anfinsen’s dogma
RCSB PDB-101 — short, illustrated explainers on structure and specific proteins, aimed at newcomers

title: 6  Session 6: Protein Structure
text:
6.3 Comparing proteins in 3D

6.3.1 Sequence alignment versus structure alignment
Session 4 defined an alignment as a hypothesis about which residues correspond. A sequence alignment decides this from the sequences alone, using substitution scores. A structure alignment decides it from the 3D coordinates, by asking which residues occupy the same position in the two folds. The notebook compares β-globin both ways with five proteins, ranging from a close paralog to an unrelated fold:



Table 6.2: Five proteins compared with β-globin, by sequence and by structure.












Compared with β-globin
Sequence identity*
Sequence-only score (shuffled max)
Residue pairs agreeing
TM-score




α-globin (human, 2HHB)
43%
288 (43)

0.88


myoglobin (human, 3RGK)
25%
111 (46)

0.91


neuroglobin (human, 1OJ6)
22%

0.82


truncated haemoglobin N (M. tuberculosis, 1IDR)

*Identity over the structurally aligned residues. “Sequence-only score” is the best Smith–Waterman alignment with BLOSUM62, and the number in brackets is the highest score among 200 alignments against shuffled versions of the same sequence. “Residue pairs agreeing” is the fraction of structurally aligned pairs that the sequence alignment also pairs up. TM-scores are normalised by the length of β-globin.
The table is best read from top to bottom. For α-globin and myoglobin, the sequence alignment has a strong signal and pairs up almost exactly the same residues as the structure alignment. (Session 5 showed that BLAST, with default settings, nevertheless missed myoglobin, because a heuristic search can skip an alignment that an exhaustive one finds.) For neuroglobin the sequence signal is still clear, but a third of the pairs are wrong, because the gaps are in the wrong places. For the bacterial truncated haemoglobin, the sequence alignment does no better than shuffled sequences and pairs up none of the right residues. The structure alignment nevertheless finds a shared globin fold over more than 100 residues. This is the central lesson: structure is more conserved than sequence. When the sequence evidence fades, structure can still reveal a relationship.


6.3.2 Measuring structural similarity: RMSD and TM-score
To compare structures, we need a number for how similar they are. RMSD (root-mean-square deviation) is the most direct measure. It is the root-mean-square distance between corresponding atoms after the two structures have been optimally superimposed. RMSD is simple, but it grows with protein length, and one badly placed loop can inflate it even when the rest of the fold matches. RMSD also depends on which atoms are compared. A superposition can be restricted to the residues that fit well, and a very low RMSD over a short fragment says nothing about the rest of the proteins. An RMSD should therefore always be given together with the number of aligned residues, for example “1.5 Å over 140 residues”. The TM-score avoids these problems. It weights each residue pair by how close it is, so that small deviations count fully and large ones hardly at all, and it normalises by protein length. It runs from 0 to 1 (identical). Unrelated proteins typically score around 0.2–0.3, and scores above about 0.5 usually mean the same overall fold. This is a rule of thumb, not a law. The truncated haemoglobin above (0.57) and GFP (0.33) are clear cases, but scores in between need other evidence.


6.3.3 DALI: comparing distance maps
If two proteins have the same fold, their distance maps should look alike, even when their sequences do not. DALI (Holm & Sander, 1993) uses this idea to compare structures. Rather than superimposing coordinates, it looks for residue correspondences that make the patterns of intramolecular distances agree.






Figure 6.3: Distance maps of β-globin, human myoglobin and GFP. The first two are almost indistinguishable although only a quarter of their residues are identical; GFP’s β-barrel gives a completely different pattern.



The analogy with sequence alignment is direct:

Sequence alignment compares residues along two sequences.
DALI compares patterns of residue–residue geometry.

DALI and TM-align (Zhang & Skolnick, 2005), which finds the superposition that maximises the TM-score, are accurate and still used for careful pairwise comparisons. They are, however, far too slow to search hundreds of millions of structures.


6.3.4 Foldseek: structure search at sequence-search speed
Session 5 ended with MMseqs2, which searches billions of sequences. Foldseek (van Kempen, Steinegger et al., 2024), from the same group, does the same for structures:



Table 6.3: Searching by sequence and by structure.






Search tool
Searches with




Sequence (Session 5)
BLAST, MMseqs2
the amino-acid sequence


Structure (this session)
Foldseek
a “structural sequence”






The key idea of Foldseek is a change of representation. For each residue, Foldseek looks at the local 3D environment (the geometry between that residue and its closest neighbour in space) and assigns one of 20 discrete structural states, the 3Di alphabet. A structure thus becomes a string of 3Di letters, one per residue. Two structures can then be compared with fast sequence-alignment machinery (the same prefilter-and-align approach as MMseqs2) instead of expensive geometric superposition:
3D coordinates
   → local geometry around each residue
   → one 3Di state per residue
   → a structural "sequence"
   → fast alignment and database search
This makes it possible to search the hundreds of millions of structures in the AlphaFold Database and the PDB in seconds to minutes. Foldseek is tens of thousands of times faster than TM-align at comparable sensitivity.






NoteMachine-learning preview: a learned representation



Nobody designed the 20 states of Foldseek’s 3Di alphabet by hand. Instead, a machine-learning model (a variational autoencoder) was trained on pairs of structurally aligned residues to find a compact set of recurring 3D environments that are conserved between related structures. You do not need to know how such a model works. The point is that a useful representation can itself be learned from data. In Session 5, humans chose both the representation (amino acids) and the scoring scheme (BLOSUM62), whereas in Foldseek, machine learning helped choose the representation. Sessions 7–12 build up the machinery behind models that learn increasingly powerful representations.


A worked comparison. We ran Foldseek locally on three structures: the two haemoglobin states used on this page (2HHB, deoxy; 1HHO, oxy) and green fluorescent protein (1EMA). Matching α-to-α or β-to-β chains between 2HHB and 1HHO, which are the same protein in two states, gives a TM-score of 0.98 and an RMSD of 0.7 Å, about as similar as two independently solved structures get. α against β globin (43% identical) still gives a TM-score of 0.90–0.91 (RMSD 1.7–1.8 Å). Searching 2HHB against GFP, in contrast, returns no hits, even with a loosened significance threshold.


6.3.5 Further reading

Wikipedia, Root-mean-square deviation of atomic positions and Template modeling score
Foldseek, GitHub and web server — try it on any PDB entry or AlphaFold model, no installation needed
DALI server, ekhidna2.biocenter.helsinki.fi/dali

title: 6  Session 6: Protein Structure
text:
6.4 Domains, complexes and conformational states

6.4.1 Structural domains
A domain is a compact, semi-independent unit of a structure, which is often able to fold on its own and is reused in many different proteins. Sessions 3 and 5 met domains from the sequence side, as Pfam families built from profile HMMs. Structural classifications instead group domains by their 3D shape, which, as the table above showed, can reveal relationships that sequence misses.
CATH (Orengo et al., 1997) classifies domains in four levels: Class (mainly α, mainly β, α/β, few secondary structures), Architecture (the overall arrangement of secondary-structure elements), Topology (how they are connected, that is, the fold), and Homologous superfamily (domains with evidence of common ancestry). β-globin’s domain is 1.10.490.10: Mainly Alpha → Orthogonal Bundle → Globin-like → Globins. So are myoglobin, neuroglobin and the M. tuberculosis truncated haemoglobin from the table above. Pfam, which works from sequence, needs a separate family for the truncated haemoglobin (PF01152, “Bacterial-like globin”, not PF00042, “Globin”) and connects the two only at the level of a clan. GFP, in contrast, is in CATH class 2 (Mainly Beta), Beta Barrel.
Three other classifications exist, each with a different philosophy: SCOP (Murzin et al., 1995; expert manual curation), ECOD (Cheng et al., 2014; organised by evolutionary relationship), and TED (Lau, Bordin et al., 2024; domains parsed automatically from the entire AlphaFold Database, hundreds of millions of predicted structures). They do not always agree on where one domain ends or on how distant superfamilies group together. Knowing that several classifications exist, and why, therefore matters more than picking one.


6.4.2 Quaternary structure, interfaces and ligands
Beyond single chains, a complex is held together by interfaces, patches of surface where two chains touch. Interfaces are usually more hydrophobic and more conserved than the rest of the surface. Many proteins also bind ligands, small molecules or ions such as haemoglobin’s haem groups. Interfaces and ligand-binding sites are where much of a protein’s function happens, and predicting them is one of the open problems of Session 12.


6.4.3 One protein, more than one structure: haemoglobin T and R
A PDB entry is one snapshot of one state. Haemoglobin has two classic states, deoxy (T, tense; 2HHB) and oxy (R, relaxed; 1HHO). Each chain hardly changes between them (TM-score 0.98), but the two α/β pairs rotate relative to each other by about 13–15° (Baldwin & Chothia, 1979; the third discussion problem measures it). The notebook measures one consequence: the distance between the iron atoms of the two β-chain haems is about 5 Å shorter in the oxy state. This quaternary change is how haemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively, since binding at one subunit makes binding at the others easier.
It follows that a PDB structure is not necessarily “the” structure of a protein. Proteins can occupy different conformational states depending on ligands, partners and conditions. This matters whenever a predicted model is compared with “the” experimental structure, and it is one of the limitations that Session 12 returns to, because AlphaFold usually predicts one state.


6.4.4 Further reading

CATH, cathdb.info; SCOP, ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/scop; ECOD, prodata.swmed.edu/ecod; TED, ted.cathdb.info
RCSB PDB-101, Hemoglobin — the T and R states, illustrated

title: 6  Session 6: Protein Structure
section: 6.5 From structure back to sequence prediction
text:
6.5 From structure back to sequence prediction

6.5.1 Secondary structure as a prediction target
Given only the sequence, could a computer predict which residues become helix, strand or coil? Stated as a learning problem, the task is:
input:   the sequence (or its profile), one window per residue
target:  H (helix), E (strand) or C (coil) for every residue
The training labels come from solved structures, assigned by DSSP as in the notebook. What information could help the prediction? The residue itself is one source, because some amino acids favour helices, others strands, and proline and glycine break both. Its neighbours in the sequence are another. A third, from Session 5, is how that position varies across homologous sequences, that is, a profile. Sessions 7–11 develop the machinery for learning such mappings, and the course returns to this problem in Sessions 7, 9 and 10 and in the capstone project.


6.5.2 Predicting the whole fold
Predicting the full 3D structure has been one of biology’s hardest problems for decades. Since 1994 the CASP competition (Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction) has tested methods blindly, on structures that are solved but not yet published. The classical strategies each build on something you have already met:

Physics (de novo or ab initio modelling) searches for the lowest-energy arrangement of the chain, using physical interactions. It is rigorous in principle, but so expensive that it long worked only for small proteins. Rosetta (Baker lab) assembles structures from short fragments of known structures, and it grew into a tool for protein design.
Comparative (homology) modelling finds a related protein of known structure (Sessions 4–5) and builds the model on it as a template. It is reliable when a template exists, but useless for a new fold. The table above shows why it works: related sequences share their structure.
Contact prediction uses the fact that residues that touch tend to mutate together. Large alignments (Session 5) therefore reveal which pairs are in contact and fill in a contact map like the one above.
Deep learning arrived with AlphaFold2 (2020), which combines learned representations, evolutionary information and geometry, and was the breakthrough in CASP14. David Baker, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein design and structure prediction. Session 12 covers AlphaFold, once Sessions 7–11 have built up the neural-network machinery.

In terms of representations, the course’s path from here is:
sequence
  → profile / evolutionary information      (Session 5)
  → learned representation                  (Sessions 7–11)
  → local structure, contacts, distances    (Sessions 7, 10, 12)
  → 3D structure                            (Session 12)

Rosetta Commons, rosettacommons.org

text:
6.9 What’s next
This session gave you structural properties that are worth predicting from sequence. Session 7 starts building the machinery to predict them. It returns to the weighted sum that a PSSM computes, \(S(x) = \sum_i w[i,
x_i]\), and formalises it as a perceptron whose weights are learned from labelled examples. It then applies the perceptron to the secondary structure you met in this session, through Rost & Sander’s PHD method, and shows why the helix you saw in PyMOL can be hard to predict from a window of residues.

title: Session 6 — Protein Structure in code
text:
Primary and quaternary structure: what’s actually in the file
▶  Open in Google Colab
This notebook fetches two real crystal structures of human hemoglobin — the deoxy (“T”, tense) state 2HHB and the oxy (“R”, relaxed) state 1HHO — and uses them to make the four levels of protein structure, and the sequence-to-structure prediction problem, concrete: primary structure is just the residue list; secondary structure is computed here from the coordinates with PyMOL and compared with the PDB entry’s own annotation; quaternary structure is measured directly as a real distance in 3D space, and that distance is shown to actually change between the two structures — the real geometric signature of hemoglobin’s allosteric mechanism. Along the way it turns the structure into a distance map and a contact map, and compares sequence alignment with structure alignment for β-globin and five other proteins, from close relatives to an unrelated fold.
Structure parsing and geometry use Biopython (Bio.PDB); secondary-structure assignment and rendering use PyMOL (open-source) as a Python library, without a window; structure alignment uses TM-align through the tmtools package.
Hemoglobin is a heterotetramer: two copies of an alpha chain and two copies of a beta chain (the same beta chain that is this course’s running example, HBB, first met on Session 3). Parsing the structure and just counting residues per chain already shows primary structure (the residue sequence itself) and sets up quaternary structure (how many chains, and which ones are identical).
parser = PDBParser(QUIET=True)
structures = {pdb_id: parser.get_structure(pdb_id, paths[pdb_id]) for pdb_id in PDB_IDS}

for pdb_id in PDB_IDS:
    print(f"--- {pdb_id.upper()} ---")
    for chain in structures[pdb_id][0]:
        protein_residues = [r for r in chain if r.id[0] == " "]
        hetero = sorted({r.get_resname() for r in chain if r.id[0] != " " and r.get_resname() != "HOH"})
        if protein_residues:
            print(f"  chain {chain.id}: {len(protein_residues)} residues, ligands={hetero}")

--- 2HHB ---
  chain A: 141 residues, ligands=['HEM']
  chain B: 146 residues, ligands=['HEM', 'PO4']
  chain C: 141 residues, ligands=['HEM']
  chain D: 146 residues, ligands=['HEM', 'PO4']
--- 1HHO ---
  chain A: 141 residues, ligands=['HEM', 'OXY', 'PO4']
  chain B: 146 residues, ligands=['HEM', 'OXY']
2HHB has all four chains (A, B, C, D) in the file directly. 1HHO’s file only contains one alpha/beta pair (A, B) — the crystal’s asymmetric unit — plus a REMARK 350 symmetry record that generates the other half of the biological tetramer. That is what a rigid-body transformation (a rotation + translation, no shape change) is for, and it matters again below when measuring a quaternary distance in 1HHO.
Both structures agree: two 141-residue alpha chains, two 146-residue beta chains, each carrying one heme group (HEM) — consistent with the real human alpha- and beta-globin sequences.

title: Session 6 — Protein Structure in code
section: Secondary structure: two ways to assign it
text:
Secondary structure: two ways to assign it
The PDB entry’s own annotation (available from EBI’s PDBe API, and used in Session 7) puts 117 of the 146 residues of HBB’s chain in alpha helices, with zero beta strands. Here the same question is answered a different way: PyMOL’s own built-in secondary-structure assignment algorithm (dss, run headlessly here, not the PDBe API) is applied directly to 2HHB’s beta chain.

from pymol import cmd              # PyMOL as a Python library, no window needed

cmd.load(paths["2hhb"], "hb")
cmd.dss("hb")                      # PyMOL's own secondary-structure assignment

ss_list = []
cmd.iterate("hb and chain B and polymer and name CA",
            "ss_list.append(ss)", space={"ss_list": ss_list})

total = len(ss_list)
helix = sum(1 for s in ss_list if s == "H")
strand = sum(1 for s in ss_list if s == "S")
print("TOTAL", total)
print("HELIX", helix)
print("STRAND", strand)
print("PCT_HELIX", round(100 * helix / total, 1))

TOTAL 146
HELIX 118
STRAND 0
PCT_HELIX 80.8


PyMOL’s dss finds 118 of 146 residues (80.8%) in a helix and 0 in a strand — a different algorithm, run on the coordinates directly rather than through PDBe’s own annotation pipeline, and it lands on essentially the same answer as the PDB entry’s annotation (117/146, ≈80%, 0 strands). The one-residue difference is just where the two algorithms draw a helix boundary at its edges — both agree HBB is an almost purely alpha-helical protein with no beta content at all, now confirmed two independent ways.

title: Session 6 — Protein Structure in code
text:
Rendering the tertiary/quaternary structure
PyMOL, used as a Python library without a window, can also render an actual image of the tetramer: cartoon representation (so alpha helices are visible directly, matching the dss numbers above), one color per chain, and the four heme iron atoms shown as spheres.

cmd.hide("everything")
cmd.show("cartoon", "polymer")
cmd.show("spheres", "resn HEM and name FE")
cmd.color("skyblue", "chain A")
cmd.color("salmon", "chain B")
cmd.color("palecyan", "chain C")
cmd.color("lightpink", "chain D")
cmd.color("orange", "resn HEM and name FE")
cmd.bg_color("white")
cmd.set("ray_opaque_background", 0)
cmd.orient("polymer")
cmd.png("_session06_2hhb_render.png", width=900, height=700, dpi=150, ray=1)

from IPython.display import Image
Image("_session06_2hhb_render.png")








Two alpha chains (blue/cyan), two beta chains (salmon/pink), all four almost entirely built from alpha helices — what the dss numbers above said — arranged around each other with four heme groups (orange spheres) roughly at the corners. That spatial arrangement of four folded chains with respect to each other is quaternary structure.

title: Session 6 — Protein Structure in code
section: A structure as a matrix: distance and contact maps
text:
A structure as a matrix: distance and contact maps
A list of 3D coordinates can be turned into a different representation: the distance between every pair of residues. For a chain of \(L\) residues this is an \(L \times L\) distance map. Thresholding it (here: Cβ atoms closer than 8 Å) gives a contact map, the definition used again in Sessions 10 and 12. Neither depends on how the protein is oriented in space, which is what makes them useful for comparing structures.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def chain_coords(structure, chain_id, atom="CA"):
    xyz = []
    for res in structure[0][chain_id]:
        if res.id[0] == " ":
            xyz.append(res[atom].coord if atom in res else res["CA"].coord)   # glycine has no CB
    return np.array(xyz)

def distance_map(xyz):
    return np.linalg.norm(xyz[:, None, :] - xyz[None, :, :], axis=-1)

d_ca = distance_map(chain_coords(structures["2hhb"], "B", "CA"))
contacts = distance_map(chain_coords(structures["2hhb"], "B", "CB")) < 8.0
L = len(d_ca)
iu = np.triu_indices(L, k=6)            # pairs at least 6 apart in sequence
print(f"beta chain: {L} residues, {contacts[iu].sum()} contacts between residues at least 6 apart in sequence")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))
im = ax[0].imshow(d_ca, cmap="viridis_r", vmax=40)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], fraction=0.046, label="Cα–Cα distance (Å)")
ax[0].set_title("distance map")
ax[1].imshow(contacts, cmap="Greys")
ax[1].set_title("contact map (Cβ–Cβ < 8 Å)")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlabel("residue"); a.set_ylabel("residue")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

beta chain: 146 residues, 197 contacts between residues at least 6 apart in sequence









The thick band along the diagonal is each helix touching itself (residue \(i\) is always close to \(i \pm 1, \dots, i \pm 4\)). The off-diagonal stripes are pairs of helices packed against each other: long-range contacts between residues far apart in sequence but close in space.

title: Session 6 — Protein Structure in code
text:
Sequence alignment versus structure alignment
A sequence alignment decides which residues correspond from the sequences alone. A structure alignment (here TM-align) decides from the 3D coordinates. Below, β-globin is compared with five proteins, from a close paralog to an unrelated fold. For each we report:

the TM-score and RMSD of the structure alignment;
the sequence identity over the structurally aligned residues;
the score of the best sequence-only local alignment (Smith–Waterman, BLOSUM62), next to the scores of 200 alignments against shuffled versions of the same sequence: is there any sequence signal at all?
how many of the structurally aligned residue pairs the sequence alignment also pairs up: does sequence alone get the correspondence right?


import random, requests
from Bio import Align
from Bio.Align import substitution_matrices
from Bio.PDB import PDBIO, Select
from tmtools import tm_align
from tmtools.io import get_structure, get_residue_data

COMPARE = [("2HHB", "A", "alpha-globin (human)"),
           ("3RGK", "A", "myoglobin (human)"),
           ("1OJ6", "A", "neuroglobin (human)"),
           ("1IDR", "A", "truncated hemoglobin N (M. tuberculosis)"),
           ("1EMA", "A", "GFP (jellyfish), unrelated fold")]

class OneChain(Select):
    def __init__(self, chain_id): self.chain_id = chain_id
    def accept_chain(self, chain): return chain.id == self.chain_id
    def accept_residue(self, res): return res.id[0] == " "

def chain_file(pdb_id, chain_id):
    """Download a PDB entry and save one chain (protein residues only) as its own file."""
    full = f"{pdb_id}.pdb"
    if not os.path.exists(full):
        r = requests.get(f"https://files.rcsb.org/download/{pdb_id}.pdb", timeout=30)
        r.raise_for_status()
        open(full, "w").write(r.text)
    out = f"{pdb_id}_{chain_id}.pdb"
    io = PDBIO(); io.set_structure(parser.get_structure(pdb_id, full)); io.save(out, OneChain(chain_id))
    return out

def load(path):
    coords, seq = get_residue_data(next(get_structure(path).get_chains()))
    return coords, seq

def aligned_pairs(a, b):
    """Residue-index pairs (i, j) matched in two gapped alignment strings."""
    pairs, i, j = set(), 0, 0
    for x, y in zip(a, b):
        if x != "-" and y != "-":
            pairs.add((i, j))
        i += x != "-"; j += y != "-"
    return pairs

aligner = Align.PairwiseAligner(mode="local", substitution_matrix=substitution_matrices.load("BLOSUM62"),
                                open_gap_score=-11, extend_gap_score=-1)

hbb_coords, hbb_seq = load(chain_file("2HHB", "B"))
random.seed(0)
print(f"{'compared with beta-globin':<42}{'TM':>6}{'RMSD':>6}{'seq id':>8}{'SW score':>10}{'shuffled max':>14}{'agree':>7}")
for pdb_id, chain_id, name in COMPARE:
    coords, seq = load(chain_file(pdb_id, chain_id))
    tm = tm_align(coords, hbb_coords, seq, hbb_seq)
    struct = aligned_pairs(tm.seqxA, tm.seqyA)
    ident = sum(seq[i] == hbb_seq[j] for i, j in struct) / len(struct)
    best = aligner.align(seq, hbb_seq)[0]
    seq_pairs = {(s1 + k, s2 + k) for (s1, e1), (s2, e2) in zip(*best.aligned) for k in range(e1 - s1)}
    shuffled = [aligner.score("".join(random.sample(seq, len(seq))), hbb_seq) for _ in range(200)]
    print(f"{name:<42}{tm.tm_norm_chain2:>6.2f}{tm.rmsd:>6.1f}{ident:>8.0%}{best.score:>10.0f}"
          f"{max(shuffled):>14.0f}{len(struct & seq_pairs) / len(struct):>7.0%}")

compared with beta-globin                     TM  RMSD  seq id  SW score  shuffled max  agree
alpha-globin (human)                        0.88   1.4     43%       288            43    95%
myoglobin (human)                           0.91   1.5     25%       111            46    97%
neuroglobin (human)                         0.82   2.0     22%        89            41    66%
truncated hemoglobin N (M. tuberculosis)    0.57   3.2     16%        28            49     0%
GFP (jellyfish), unrelated fold             0.33   5.1      6%        25            50     0%


TM-scores are normalized by the length of β-globin. Read the table from top to bottom:

Alpha-globin and myoglobin: the sequence alignment score is far above anything the shuffled sequences reach, and the sequence alignment pairs up almost exactly the same residues as the structure alignment.
Neuroglobin: still a clear sequence signal, but only about two thirds of the residue pairs agree; the sequence alignment has put gaps in the wrong places.
Truncated hemoglobin: the sequence alignment scores no better than shuffled sequences, and it pairs up none of the right residues. The structure alignment still finds a shared fold (TM-score well above GFP’s) over more than 100 residues: structure is more conserved than sequence.
GFP: a low TM-score; the structures have nothing in common.

title: Session 6 — Protein Structure in code
text:
Measuring a real quaternary-structure distance
A concrete geometric property, rather than just a picture: the distance between the iron atoms of the two beta-chain hemes. This distance is the classic textbook signature of hemoglobin’s allosteric mechanism (Baldwin & Chothia, 1979) — it should be larger in the deoxygenated (“T”, tense) state than in the oxygenated (“R”, relaxed) state, since the whole point of the T→R quaternary shift is that the two beta chains move closer together as oxygen binds.
First, all six pairwise Fe–Fe distances within 2HHB (T-state), which is small enough to have all four chains directly in one file:

fe_2hhb = {}
for chain in structures["2hhb"][0]:
    for res in chain:
        if res.get_resname() == "HEM":
            fe_2hhb[chain.id] = res["FE"].get_coord()

print("2HHB (deoxy, T-state) pairwise Fe-Fe distances:")
for a, b in itertools.combinations(sorted(fe_2hhb), 2):
    d = np.linalg.norm(fe_2hhb[a] - fe_2hhb[b])
    print(f"  {a}-{b}: {d:.2f} A")

beta_beta_T = np.linalg.norm(fe_2hhb["B"] - fe_2hhb["D"])
print(f"\nBeta-beta Fe-Fe distance, T-state (2HHB): {beta_beta_T:.2f} A")

2HHB (deoxy, T-state) pairwise Fe-Fe distances:
  A-B: 36.49 A
  A-C: 34.16 A
  A-D: 24.35 A
  B-C: 24.26 A
  B-D: 39.51 A
  C-D: 36.42 A

Beta-beta Fe-Fe distance, T-state (2HHB): 39.51 A


1HHO’s file only has one alpha/beta pair, so getting the other beta chain means actually applying the rigid-body transformation from the file’s REMARK 350 record — the same kind of operation, in miniature, that structure-comparison tools like RMSD or TM-align (mentioned on the book page) use to superimpose whole structures onto each other.

fe_1hho = {}
for chain in structures["1hho"][0]:
    for res in chain:
        if res.get_resname() == "HEM":
            fe_1hho[chain.id] = res["FE"].get_coord()

# REMARK 350 BIOMT for the second copy in 1HHO's biological tetramer:
# swap x and y, negate z, no translation.
R = np.array([[0, 1, 0],
              [1, 0, 0],
              [0, 0, -1]])

fe_B = np.array(fe_1hho["B"], dtype=float)
fe_B_symmetry_mate = R @ fe_B

beta_beta_R = np.linalg.norm(fe_B - fe_B_symmetry_mate)
print(f"Beta-beta Fe-Fe distance, R-state (1HHO): {beta_beta_R:.2f} A")
print(f"Beta-beta Fe-Fe distance, T-state (2HHB): {beta_beta_T:.2f} A")
print(f"Contraction going deoxy (T) -> oxy (R):    {beta_beta_T - beta_beta_R:.2f} A")

Beta-beta Fe-Fe distance, R-state (1HHO): 34.62 A
Beta-beta Fe-Fe distance, T-state (2HHB): 39.51 A
Contraction going deoxy (T) -> oxy (R):    4.89 A


Two independently solved crystal structures of the same protein, in its two functional states, show the two beta hemes roughly 5 Å closer together in the oxygenated state than in the deoxygenated one — a real, measured instance of the T→R quaternary transition, not just a textbook diagram. This is also the kind of number a quaternary structure-comparison metric (Ligand RMSD, interface RMSD, …) is built to summarize systematically across many structures at once, rather than one hand-picked distance at a time.

title: 7  Session 7: Linear Models, Gradient Descent, the XOR Problem & Secondary Structure Prediction
section: 7.2 Two pictures to keep in mind
text:
7.2 Two pictures to keep in mind
This session uses many names: profile score (PSSM), perceptron, linear and logistic regression, sigmoid, tanh, hidden layer, multilayer perceptron and PHD. Behind them there are only two pictures, and together these two pictures explain the whole idea of the lecture.






Figure 7.1: Top: one weighted sum followed by an activation. A PSSM score, a perceptron and logistic regression are all this picture, and all of them draw one straight boundary. Bottom: a hidden layer of weighted sums with a nonlinear activation, followed by one more weighted sum. This is a multilayer perceptron (MLP), such as PHD, and it can combine several boundaries.



Keep them in mind as you read. The goal of the session is to understand what changes between the two pictures, and why that change makes XOR possible.
crumbs: 7  Session 7: Linear Models, Gradient Descent, the XOR Problem & Secondary Structure Prediction

title: 7  Session 7: Linear Models, Gradient Descent, the XOR Problem & Secondary Structure Prediction
section: 7.3 A profile score and a perceptron: the same weighted sum
text:
7.3 A profile score and a perceptron: the same weighted sum
You actually already know the central computation of a neural network. Session 5 introduced the profile score, which checks how well a sequence matches a known family. It multiplies each position’s observed value by a position-specific weight and adds up the results. In Session 1’s terms, this is a dot product, something you learned on the first day. A perceptron has exactly the same mathematical core, because it also computes a weighted sum \(z\):
\[
z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_n x_n + b
\]
The extra term \(b\), a bias, shifts the whole sum by a constant amount, so that the model’s decision threshold can sit somewhere other than zero. The PSSM and the perceptron share this weighted sum, but they differ in what they do with it. A PSSM reports the sum itself as a score. A perceptron instead passes the sum through an activation function, originally a threshold (output 1 if \(z > 0\), else 0), to make a classification. Keeping the two terms apart helps later on. “Profile score” means a linear score, and “perceptron” means a (thresholded) classifier that adds an activation function to the same weighted sum.
Where the name comes from. Frank Rosenblatt introduced the perceptron in 1958, first as a simulation on an IBM 704 computer, and the Mark I Perceptron machine followed in 1960. He modelled it on a simplified neuron. Each synapse weights its input, the cell sums the weighted inputs, and the cell fires once the sum crosses a threshold. The weights \(w_i\) therefore stand for connection strengths, and \(b\) for how easily the cell fires. His own diagram set the circuit of the brain next to the perceptron built to mirror it:






Figure 7.2: Rosenblatt’s own 1958 diagram: a biological brain’s circuit (top) next to the perceptron he built to mirror it (bottom) — retina/sensory input, an association layer, and motor/response output on both sides. Public domain (US federal government work) — Rosenblatt, F., “The Design of an Intelligent Automaton,” Research Reviews, Office of Naval Research, October 1958, pp. 5-13.



Geometrically, \(z = 0\) is a line in two dimensions (a plane, or hyperplane, in higher dimensions), and this line is the model’s decision boundary. On one side of it the output is 1, and on the other side it is 0.
Solving \(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b = 0\) for \(x_2\) gives \(x_2 = -\frac{w_1}{w_2} x_1 - \frac{b}{w_2}\). This is the familiar \(y = mx + c\) form of a line, with the bias \(b\) playing the role of the intercept \(c\) (scaled by \(-1/w_2\)). Changing \(b\) therefore slides the whole line sideways without changing its slope. The intercept \(b_0\) plays the same role in ordinary linear regression, as the next section shows.

Wikipedia, Perceptron — other activation functions and the original biological motivation, beyond the general-purpose version above

title: 7  Session 7: Linear Models, Gradient Descent, the XOR Problem & Secondary Structure Prediction
text:
7.4 Learning the weights from examples
So far the weights have simply been given. A profile’s weights come from counting: we look at a multiple alignment, count how often each residue appears at each position, and turn those counts into log-odds scores. This works well when we already have a trustworthy alignment to count from. As Session 5 showed, small alignments need some extra tricks (pseudocounts), but that is still counting, only with some modifications.
The alternative to counting, and the one the rest of this course builds on, is to learn the weights directly from labelled examples with an optimisation method, normally gradient descent as described in Session 1. We often start with arbitrary (random) weights and measure how wrong the model’s current predictions are with a loss function. We then compute the gradient of that loss with respect to each weight, and nudge every weight a small step in the direction that reduces the loss. This is repeated many times. No alignment and no hand-counting are needed, only examples and many small corrections. This is the foundation of all machine learning: we do not tell the computer what to do, but let it learn what to do.
In this session’s lab, the code works directly with raw tensors and automatic differentiation (Session 2). It deliberately avoids the higher-level nn.Module and training-loop tools that Session 8 introduces, because the point here is to see every step of the mechanics rather than to use a convenient shortcut around them.
Worked example. Take a perceptron with one input and no bias yet (\(z = wx\)), an initial weight \(w_0 = 0\), a training example \((x, y) = (2, 6)\), a squared-error loss \(L(w) = (wx - y)^2\), and a learning rate \(\eta = 0.05\). Session 1’s chain rule gives
\[
\frac{dL}{dw} = 2(wx - y) \cdot x
\]
The table shows the first iterations of gradient descent, \(w_{n+1} = w_n - \eta \, dL/dw\):



Table 7.1: The first iterations of gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta = 0.05\).

The weight converges towards \(w = 3\) (Figure 7.3), where the prediction \(wx = 3 \times 2 = 6\) would exactly match the target. Just as in Session 1’s one-variable example, the size of each correction (\(dL/dw\)) shrinks by itself as the prediction gets closer, so \(\eta\) needs no manual adjustment. This holds only as long as the learning rate is not too large. With an excessive learning rate, gradient descent overshoots the minimum and can oscillate or diverge (Session 1’s second discussion problem).
Deriving vs. learning, on the simplest possible model. Ordinary linear regression, which fits a line \(\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x\) to data, has a direct numerical solution. It therefore makes a useful check, because gradient descent should reach the same optimum iteratively. Take five noisy points roughly following \(y \approx 2x\), with \(x = (1,2,3,4,5)\) and \(y = (2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1)\). A least-squares solver gives \(b_0 = 0.05\) and \(b_1 = 1.99\) in one step, and gradient descent (learning rate \(\eta = 0.01\), thousands of small steps) converges to the same \(b_0 = 0.050\) and \(b_1 = 1.990\).
This mirrors the contrast between Session 5’s PSSM, whose weights are derived directly from alignment counts, and this session’s gradient descent, whose weights are learned iteratively. Gradient descent is what the rest of the course uses, because most models, including a perceptron with its classification loss, have no direct solution.






NoteOptional: the formula





The least-squares solution can be written with the normal equations. We stack the inputs into a matrix \(X\), with a column of 1s for \(b_0\) next to the \(x\) values. Then
\[
\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}
\]
This formula is a way to write the solution, not a way to compute it, because numerical libraries (np.linalg.lstsq, scikit-learn) use more stable methods than inverting \(X^\top X\). Moreover, when the columns of \(X\) are exactly linearly dependent, \(X^\top X\) cannot be inverted at all. This session’s lab comes close to that case. The 20 amino-acid fractions of a protein sum to 1 (for 54 of its 55 proteins, since one contains unknown residues), so together with the intercept column they are almost exactly linearly dependent. A least-squares solver still finds a best fit, but the individual weights are poorly determined.

section: 7.5 What one weighted sum can represent
text:
7.5 What one weighted sum can represent
Before asking what a perceptron cannot do, it helps to see what it can do.
A perceptron first computes a weighted sum of its inputs, \(z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b\), which is any real number. To turn that number into a decision, it passes \(z\) through an activation function. The simplest one is the step function:
\[
\text{step}(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } z > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\]
The step function answers yes or no, and nothing in between. The weighted sum says how strongly the evidence points one way, and the step throws that strength away and keeps only the sign. This is why a perceptron draws a straight boundary: \(z > 0\) on one side, \(z \le 0\) on the other, and the line \(z = 0\) between them. We use the step function here because it makes the logic gates below exact and easy to check by hand. It has one fatal flaw, which Session 8 returns to: its slope is zero everywhere it is defined, so gradient descent gets no signal from it and cannot train a network through it. Every activation used later in the course — sigmoid, tanh, ReLU — is a smoothed version of this same idea.
With a step activation, a single perceptron can implement basic logic gates directly. No training is required, only weights chosen by hand:



Table 7.2: Perceptron weights, chosen by hand, that implement three logic gates.

Take AND as an example. At \((1,1)\), \(z = 1+1-1.5 = 0.5 > 0 \to 1\), and at every other corner \(z \le -0.5 \to 0\), which is exactly the truth table of AND. (NAND is AND with both weights and the bias negated, which flips every output.) In the notebook, all three gates check out exactly against their truth tables.
Each gate is one straight decision boundary through the square of four inputs, with the “1” corners on one side and the “0” corners on the other. For AND, only \((1,1)\) lies on the positive side of the line \(x_1 + x_2 = 1.5\). The second discussion problem asks you to find weights for OR yourself.
This is easiest to see if we draw the four inputs as dots on a plane and the decision boundary \(z = 0\) as a line between them. The step activation then simply asks on which side of the line a dot lies:

The green line is the decision boundary \(z = 0\); on the shaded side \(z > 0\). For AND the line cuts off one corner, for OR it cuts off the opposite corner, and NAND is AND with the sides swapped.

7.6 What one weighted sum can never represent: XOR
A model built purely from weighted sums has a real limitation, because there is a whole class of patterns it can never represent, however its weights are chosen. The classic illustration is the XOR problem. XOR is a function of two binary inputs that outputs 1 when its inputs differ and 0 when they are the same.



Table 7.3: The XOR function.

\(x_2\)
XOR

Before reading on, try it: find weights \(w_1, w_2, b\) that reproduce this table with one perceptron. You will not succeed. The two “1” outputs sit on opposite corners of the input square, and no straight line can put both of them on one side while leaving both “0” outputs on the other. Section 4 of the notebook tries 226,981 combinations of \(w_1\), \(w_2\) and \(b\) (every value from −3 to 3 in steps of 0.1). About 5,000 of them reproduce AND, 9,500 OR and 4,500 NAND, but not one reproduces XOR.






Figure 7.5: A linear model trained on XOR (left) settles on predicting 0.5 everywhere. Every straight-line boundary it could draw leaves at least one point on the wrong side, so gradient descent settles for the least-wrong compromise. A hidden-layer model on the same data (right) combines two linear boundaries into a non-linear one that separates all four points correctly. Both panels show the notebook’s own trained models, not illustrative sketches.









NoteOptional: the algebraic proof





The geometric argument can be turned into a short proof. A perceptron with a sign-style activation outputs 1 when \(z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b > 0\) and 0 otherwise. Reproducing the XOR table therefore requires all four of the following inequalities:
\[
b \le 0, \qquad w_1 + b > 0, \qquad w_2 + b > 0, \qquad w_1 + w_2 + b \le 0
\]
The first and last inequalities come from the two “0” rows, and the middle two from the “1” rows. Adding the second and third inequalities gives \(w_1 + w_2 + 2b > 0\), that is, \(w_1 + w_2 + b > -b \ge 0\) (using \(b \le 0\) from the first inequality). The fourth inequality, however, says directly that \(w_1 + w_2 + b \le 0\). No values of \(w_1\), \(w_2\) and \(b\) can satisfy both at once, so no such weights exist. This is the same fact that the geometric picture showed, derived without drawing anything.




7.6.1 Further reading

Wikipedia, Linear separability — generalises the geometric argument above beyond the two-input case shown here

The last column is XOR. Take \((1,1)\) as an example. Both inputs are on, so the OR unit fires (\(z = 1.5\)), but the NAND unit does not (\(z = -0.5\)). The output unit then sees \(h_1 + h_2 = 1\), and since \(1 - 1.5 < 0\), \(y = 0\). Only the two mixed inputs switch on both hidden units, and only then does the AND unit fire.
The same calculation can be written in matrix form for all four inputs at once, with the inputs as the rows of \(X\) and one column of \(W_1\) per hidden unit:
\[
H = \text{step}(X W_1 + \mathbf{b}_1), \qquad
W_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{b}_1 = (-0.5,\ 1.5)
\]
\[
\mathbf{y} = \text{step}(H W_2 + b_2), \qquad
W_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad b_2 = -1.5
\]
Section 5 of the notebook does exactly this in PyTorch and prints every intermediate value, and the result is the table above.
The two perceptrons computing OR and NAND form a hidden layer, and the third perceptron, which combines their outputs, gives the model’s final output. The notebook’s hidden-layer network has the same shape (two hidden units feeding one output unit), but it finds its weights by gradient descent rather than by hand. Seeing both, an exact hand-built solution here and a learned approximate one later, makes clear that gradient descent is not discovering some exotic new trick. It finds weights for a structure that could, in principle, be written down directly.

7.7.1 The activation must be nonlinear
The construction above works only because each unit applies a nonlinear activation (here a step) before its output is passed on. Without one, stacking layers gains nothing. To see why, we take the equations above and simply leave the step out, keeping the same convention of one input per row: the hidden layer is \(H = X W_1 + \mathbf{b}_1\) and the output is \(\mathbf{z} = H W_2 + b_2\). Then
\[
\mathbf{z} = (X W_1 + \mathbf{b}_1) W_2 + b_2 = X\,(W_1 W_2) + (\mathbf{b}_1 W_2 + b_2)
\]
which is again a single weighted sum of the inputs, with one matrix \(W_1 W_2\) and one bias. Any number of linear layers therefore collapses into one linear layer, and one linear layer cannot solve XOR. A nonlinear activation between the layers (a step, sigmoid, tanh or ReLU) is what lets the hidden units bend the decision boundary. The notebook shows this directly. The same two-hidden-unit network, trained on XOR with the activation removed, gets stuck at 0.5 for every input, just like the plain linear model.

TipA short history



Minsky and Papert’s book Perceptrons (1969) proved rigorously that single-layer perceptrons cannot solve problems like XOR. It is widely credited with contributing to a drop in neural-network research in the 1970s, the first “AI winter”. Multi-layer networks were known to be more powerful, but training them became practical only with backpropagation (popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams in 1986), which applies Session 1’s chain rule through the hidden layers. Session 9 covers it.

title: 7  Session 7: Linear Models, Gradient Descent, the XOR Problem & Secondary Structure Prediction
text:
7.8 Biological analogues

7.8.1 Interactions between positions: Bulyk et al.
XOR is not just a toy puzzle about logic gates, because the same structure shows up in real sequence motifs. Bulyk, Johnson & Church (2002) used protein-binding microarrays to measure how the binding affinity of a zinc-finger transcription factor depended on the nucleotides at different positions of its binding site. They found that the positions do not contribute independently, since the effect of the nucleotide at one position depends on what is at another position. This directly violates the assumption behind a profile score, namely that the contribution of each position can simply be added to the others. They measured the zinc-finger protein Zif268 (mouse Egr1) and mutants of it binding to all 64 possible central triplets of its site, and concluded that neither a consensus sequence nor a position weight matrix describes the protein’s true specificity.
To see why this kind of dependency is an XOR-shaped problem, consider a deliberately simplified, illustrative version. It is not the actual data from the paper, which involve more positions and continuous binding affinities, but it has the same qualitative shape. Suppose a two-position motif binds strongly only when the two positions belong to different purine/pyrimidine classes (one purine, R = A or G, and one pyrimidine, Y = C or T), and weakly when they belong to the same class:



Table 7.7: Binding strength depending on the purine/pyrimidine classes of two positions.





Position 1
Position 2
Binding
