title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
text:
Part 1 — What does it mean to learn from data?
▶  Open in Google Colab
This notebook follows the session’s three parts:
Session 7 asked what a model can represent. This session asks the question that matters in practice: how do we know whether a model has learned anything useful?
Supervised learning fits a model to labelled examples: inputs whose correct answer is already known. Unsupervised learning looks for structure in data without labels, for example clustering sequences into families. Everything from Session 5 onward is supervised. Supervised problems come in two kinds, depending on what the label is:
Below are two real examples, one of each.

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
section: A regression problem: helix fraction from composition
text:
A regression problem: helix fraction from composition
The same 55 PDB entries as the Session 7 lab, fetched live from EBI’s PDBe API. Here we use a single feature: the fraction of the sequence made up of residues with a Chou-Fasman helix propensity of at least 1.1 (E, M, A, L, K, F, Q). The target is the real fraction of residues in helices.

PDB_IDS = ['21XG', '38LJ', '9WRU', '9NVT', '9XZ9', '7ILS', '9RYL', '9TLR', '32TC', '13DZ', '9TCX', '9YBX', '9N2Y', '29OL', '9PNX', '9YMO', '9HWE', '9RPQ', '9RR6', '9W2A', '21LO', '9RK7', '9OU3', '9P39', '9T4I', '9VOM', '9W28', '9RFG', '9V5C', '9RQP', '9I4O', '9QWL', '9QYO', '9WM8', '9QRF', '9X6R', '9TZG', '9QGV', '9U97', '9YK5', '9IC9', '9XPD', '9DJF', '9DJR', '9NK4', '9NCE', '9I1B', '9RQQ', '7IPN', '9LCS', '9Z70', '9KZN', '9SI4', '9P45', '9FD0']
HELIX_FORMERS = "EMALKFQ"   # Chou-Fasman helix propensity >= 1.1

def fetch_helix_fraction(pdbid):
    lo = pdbid.lower()
    r = requests.get(f"https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/api/pdb/entry/molecules/{lo}", timeout=15)
    r.raise_for_status()
    mol = [m for m in r.json()[lo] if m.get("molecule_type") == "polypeptide(L)" and m.get("sequence")][0]
    seq, chain_id, length = mol["sequence"], mol["in_chains"][0], mol["length"]
    r = requests.get(f"https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/api/pdb/entry/secondary_structure/{lo}", timeout=15)
    r.raise_for_status()
    helices = []
    for molecule in r.json()[lo]["molecules"]:
        for chain in molecule["chains"]:
            if chain["chain_id"] == chain_id:
                helices = chain["secondary_structure"].get("helices", [])
    n_helix = sum(h["end"]["residue_number"] - h["start"]["residue_number"] + 1 for h in helices)
    return seq, n_helix / length

helix_seqs, helix_frac = [], []
for pdbid in PDB_IDS:
    s, h = fetch_helix_fraction(pdbid)
    helix_seqs.append(s); helix_frac.append(h)
helix_frac = np.array(helix_frac)
former_frac = np.array([sum(s.count(a) for a in HELIX_FORMERS) / len(s) for s in helix_seqs])
print(f"{len(helix_frac)} proteins; helix fraction ranges {helix_frac.min():.2f}-{helix_frac.max():.2f}")
r, p = pearsonr(former_frac, helix_frac)
print(f"Pearson r between helix-former content and helix fraction: {r:.2f} (p = {p:.1e})")

55 proteins; helix fraction ranges 0.03-0.84
Pearson r between helix-former content and helix fraction: 0.71 (p = 1.3e-09)

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
section: A classification problem: secreted or nuclear?
text:
A classification problem: secreted or nuclear?
Today’s main dataset: reviewed human proteins from UniProt with exactly one annotated subcellular location, in five classes. It is fetched live once here and reused for the rest of the notebook. Accessions are kept because Part 2 needs them.

UNIPROT_CLASSES = {
    "Cytoplasm": "SL-0086",
    "Nucleus": "SL-0191",
    "Mitochondrion": "SL-0173",
    "Secreted": "SL-0243",
    "Cell membrane": "SL-0039",
}
CLASS_NAMES = list(UNIPROT_CLASSES.keys())

def fetch_uniprot(sl_code, size=500):   # only the first 500 hits, to keep the download small
    query = f"organism_id:9606 AND reviewed:true AND cc_scl_term:{sl_code} AND length:[50 TO 500]"
    r = requests.get(
        "https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/search",
        params={"query": query, "fields": "accession,sequence,cc_subcellular_location",
                "format": "tsv", "size": size},
        timeout=60,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    rows = []
    for line in r.text.strip().split("\n")[1:]:
        parts = line.split("\t")
        if len(parts) == 3:
            rows.append(tuple(parts))  # (accession, sequence, location_text)
    return rows

def is_unambiguous_single_location(location_text, target):
    '''Keep only entries whose SUBCELLULAR LOCATION comment names exactly
    one location term (matching the target), ignoring free-text Notes,
    evidence-code tags, and skipping isoform-specific annotations.'''
    location_text = re.sub(r"Note=.*", "", location_text)
    location_text = re.sub(r"\{[^}]*\}", "", location_text)
    if "Isoform" in location_text:
        return False
    terms = set()
    for statement in [s.strip() for s in location_text.split(".") if s.strip()]:
        body = statement.split(":", 1)[-1] if ":" in statement else statement
        top_term = re.split(r"[,;]", body)[0].strip()
        if top_term:
            terms.add(top_term)
    return len(terms) == 1 and next(iter(terms)) == target

entries_by_class = {}
for class_name, sl_code in UNIPROT_CLASSES.items():
    raw = fetch_uniprot(sl_code)
    clean = [(acc, seq) for acc, seq, loc in raw if is_unambiguous_single_location(loc, class_name)]
    entries_by_class[class_name] = clean
    print(f"{class_name:15s} raw hits: {len(raw):4d}   unambiguous single-location: {len(clean):4d}")

Cytoplasm       raw hits:  500   unambiguous single-location:  424
Nucleus         raw hits:  500   unambiguous single-location:  497
Mitochondrion   raw hits:  500   unambiguous single-location:  140
Secreted        raw hits:  500   unambiguous single-location:  488
Cell membrane   raw hits:  500   unambiguous single-location:  338


To be able to plot a classification problem, take just two classes (secreted vs. nuclear) and two biologically motivated features:

mean Kyte-Doolittle hydrophobicity of the first 25 residues (secreted proteins start with a hydrophobic signal peptide, Session 11);
the fraction of lysine + arginine (nuclear localization signals and DNA/RNA binding are rich in K/R).

Logistic regression is the classic classifier: the same weighted sum \(z = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b\) as Session 7’s perceptron, passed through the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\), which maps it to a number between 0 and 1. Because logistic regression is fitted with the log-loss (cross-entropy), that number can be read as an estimate of \(P(\text{secreted}\mid x)\); how well calibrated it is still has to be checked on held-out data. The decision boundary is where \(P = 0.5\), i.e. \(z = 0\), the same straight line as the perceptron’s.

KD = {'A': 1.8, 'R': -4.5, 'N': -3.5, 'D': -3.5, 'C': 2.5, 'Q': -3.5, 'E': -3.5, 'G': -0.4,
      'H': -3.2, 'I': 4.5, 'L': 3.8, 'K': -3.9, 'M': 1.9, 'F': 2.8, 'P': -1.6, 'S': -0.8,
      'T': -0.7, 'W': -0.9, 'Y': -1.3, 'V': 4.2}
def nterm_hydrophobicity(seq, n=25):
    return np.mean([KD.get(a, 0.0) for a in seq[:n]])
def frac_KR(seq):
    return (seq.count("K") + seq.count("R")) / len(seq)

two = [(s, 1) for _, s in entries_by_class["Secreted"]] + [(s, 0) for _, s in entries_by_class["Nucleus"]]
X2 = np.array([[nterm_hydrophobicity(s), frac_KR(s)] for s, _ in two])
y2 = np.array([lab for _, lab in two])
X2_tr, X2_te, y2_tr, y2_te = train_test_split(X2, y2, test_size=0.25, stratify=y2, random_state=0)
logreg = LogisticRegression().fit(X2_tr, y2_tr)
print(f"{len(y2)} proteins ({y2.sum()} secreted, {(1 - y2).sum()} nuclear)")
print(f"held-out accuracy of logistic regression: {logreg.score(X2_te, y2_te):.3f}")

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
section: A running toy example: 3×3 pixel patterns
text:
A running toy example: 3×3 pixel patterns
Magnus Ekman’s Learning Deep Learning (ch. 2) trains perceptrons to recognise tiny 3×3 pixel patterns. We reuse the idea as the smallest possible classification problem: nine inputs (dark = +1, light = −1) and five classes. Every example is a clean pattern plus Gaussian noise (σ = 0.8 per pixel). “Cross” deliberately shares its middle row with “horizontal” and its middle column with “vertical”, so some confusions are expected.

PATTERNS = {
    "horizontal":    [[0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0]],
    "vertical":      [[0, 1, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 1, 0]],
    "diagonal":      [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]],
    "anti-diagonal": [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0]],
    "cross":         [[0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0]],
}
PAT_NAMES = list(PATTERNS)
CLEAN = np.array([np.where(np.array(p).flatten() == 1, 1.0, -1.0) for p in PATTERNS.values()])
SIGMA = 0.8

def sample_patterns(n_per_class, rng, sigma=SIGMA):
    y = np.repeat(np.arange(len(PAT_NAMES)), n_per_class)
    X = CLEAN[y] + rng.normal(0, sigma, (len(y), 9))
    return X, y

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X_demo, y_demo = sample_patterns(2, rng)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 5, figsize=(8, 5))
for c, name in enumerate(PAT_NAMES):
    axes[0, c].imshow(-CLEAN[c].reshape(3, 3), cmap="gray", vmin=-2, vmax=2)
    axes[0, c].set_title(name, fontsize=9)
    for k in range(2):
        axes[k + 1, c].imshow(-X_demo[y_demo == c][k].reshape(3, 3), cmap="gray", vmin=-2, vmax=2)
for ax in axes.flat:
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("clean"); axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("noisy"); axes[2, 0].set_ylabel("noisy")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(f"{FIGS}/session08-3x3-patterns.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
section: Training, validation and test sets, on the 3×3 problem
text:
Training, validation and test sets, on the 3×3 problem

Training set: used to fit the weights.
Validation set: used to make choices (here: how many epochs to train) without touching the test set.
Test set: used once, at the end, to report the final number.

The classifier is five Session 7 perceptrons, one per pattern, each trained with the perceptron rule to output +1 for its own pattern and −1 for the rest (“one-vs-rest”). The predicted class is the perceptron with the highest score \(z\). There is no hidden layer, so no backpropagation is needed.

rng = np.random.RandomState(1)
X_tr, y_tr = sample_patterns(20, rng)    # 100 training examples
X_va, y_va = sample_patterns(20, rng)    # 100 validation examples
X_te, y_te = sample_patterns(40, rng)    # 200 test examples
add_bias = lambda X: np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]

def train_one_vs_rest(X, y, epochs, eta=0.1, seed=0):
    r = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    W = r.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, (len(PAT_NAMES), 10))
    Xb = add_bias(X)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for i in r.permutation(len(Xb)):
            for c in range(len(PAT_NAMES)):
                target = 1 if y[i] == c else -1
                if np.sign(W[c] @ Xb[i]) != target:
                    W[c] += eta * target * Xb[i]       # Session 7's perceptron update
    return W

scores = lambda W, X: add_bias(X) @ W.T
predict = lambda W, X: scores(W, X).argmax(axis=1)

# Train once for 50 epochs and record the accuracy after every epoch.
# (Training for k epochs from the same seed follows exactly this path, so epoch k here = a k-epoch model.)
def train_with_history(X, y, epochs, eta=0.1, seed=0):
    r = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    W = r.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, (len(PAT_NAMES), 10))
    Xb = add_bias(X)
    history = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for i in r.permutation(len(Xb)):
            for c in range(len(PAT_NAMES)):
                target = 1 if y[i] == c else -1
                if np.sign(W[c] @ Xb[i]) != target:
                    W[c] += eta * target * Xb[i]
        history.append(((predict(W, X_tr) == y_tr).mean(), (predict(W, X_va) == y_va).mean()))
    return np.array(history)

hist = train_with_history(X_tr, y_tr, 50)
train_curve, val_curve = hist[:, 0], hist[:, 1]
epochs_axis = np.arange(1, 51)
print("epochs   train acc   validation acc")
for e in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
    print(f"{e:6d}   {train_curve[e-1]:9.3f}   {val_curve[e-1]:14.3f}")
print(f"\ntraining accuracy over the 50 epochs: {train_curve.min():.2f} to {train_curve.max():.2f}")
print(f"validation accuracy over the 50 epochs: {val_curve.min():.2f} to {val_curve.max():.2f} "
      f"(best single epoch: {val_curve.argmax() + 1}, {val_curve.max():.2f})")

# How noisy is one validation accuracy? With n = 100 examples and accuracy near 0.9,
# its standard error is sqrt(p(1-p)/n):
se = np.sqrt(0.9 * 0.1 / len(y_va))
plateau = val_curve.mean()
print(f"standard error of one validation accuracy (n = {len(y_va)}): about {se:.2f}")
print(f"plateau (mean validation accuracy over all epochs): {plateau:.3f}")

# The rule: the fewest epochs whose validation accuracy reaches the plateau.
best_epochs = int(epochs_axis[np.argmax(val_curve >= plateau)])
W_pat = train_one_vs_rest(X_tr, y_tr, best_epochs)
test_pred = predict(W_pat, X_te)
test_acc = (test_pred == y_te).mean()
print(f"\nchosen on validation: {best_epochs} epochs (validation accuracy {val_curve[best_epochs-1]:.2f})")
print(f"test accuracy, measured once: {test_acc:.3f}")

epochs   train acc   validation acc
     1       0.890            0.840
     2       0.880            0.900
     3       0.920            0.940
     5       0.940            0.900
    10       0.930            0.890
    20       0.900            0.880
    50       0.950            0.900

training accuracy over the 50 epochs: 0.88 to 0.98
validation accuracy over the 50 epochs: 0.84 to 0.94 (best single epoch: 3, 0.94)
standard error of one validation accuracy (n = 100): about 0.03
plateau (mean validation accuracy over all epochs): 0.894

chosen on validation: 2 epochs (validation accuracy 0.90)
test accuracy, measured once: 0.895



fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
ax.plot(epochs_axis, train_curve, "o-", ms=3, color="grey", label="training accuracy")
ax.plot(epochs_axis, val_curve, "o-", ms=3, color="tab:blue", label="validation accuracy")
ax.axhspan(plateau - se, plateau + se, color="tab:blue", alpha=0.12,
           label=f"plateau {plateau:.2f} ± one standard error ({se:.2f})")
ax.axhline(plateau, color="tab:blue", lw=1, ls="--")
ax.axvline(best_epochs, color="tab:orange", lw=1.5)
ax.plot(best_epochs, test_acc, "*", ms=14, color="tab:orange",
        label=f"chosen: {best_epochs} epochs; test accuracy, measured once: {test_acc:.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel("epochs of training"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy")
ax.set_ylim(0.8, 1.0); ax.set_xlim(0, 51)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.17), ncol=2, fontsize=8.5, frameon=False)
ax.set_title("3×3 perceptrons: accuracy after every epoch")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(f"{FIGS}/session08-3x3-epochs.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()








Two things to see in this plot:

Training accuracy never settles. The noisy patterns overlap, so no set of straight lines separates all of them, and the perceptron rule keeps changing the weights for every misclassified example.
Validation accuracy is noisy too. From epoch 2 on it moves around a plateau, and most of the epoch-to-epoch movement is within the noise of an accuracy measured on only 100 examples (the shaded band). The single best epoch (3, 0.94) is partly luck: picking the maximum of 50 noisy numbers gives an optimistic estimate: selection bias. (Choosing on the validation set is what it is for; the bias is in reporting the best score as the expected one.) We use the earliest epoch that has clearly reached the plateau, rather than chasing the highest noisy value.

The test set is then used once, for the chosen model.

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
text:
Evaluating a classifier
Accuracy alone hides which mistakes are made. The confusion matrix (rows = true class, columns = predicted class) shows them. For each class \(c\), treated as “positive” against the rest:
\[
\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP} \qquad
\text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN} \qquad
F_1 = \frac{2\cdot\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}}{\text{precision}+\text{recall}}
\]
\[
\text{MCC} = \frac{TP\cdot TN - FP\cdot FN}{\sqrt{(TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)}}
\]

cm = confusion_matrix(y_te, test_pred)
print("confusion matrix (rows = true, columns = predicted):")
print(" " * 15 + " ".join(f"{n[:6]:>6s}" for n in PAT_NAMES))
for name, row in zip(PAT_NAMES, cm):
    print(f"{name:>14s} " + " ".join(f"{v:6d}" for v in row))

prec, rec, f1, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(y_te, test_pred, zero_division=0)
print("\nper class:        precision  recall   F1     MCC (class vs rest)")
for c, name in enumerate(PAT_NAMES):
    mcc_c = matthews_corrcoef(y_te == c, test_pred == c)
    print(f"{name:>14s}   {prec[c]:9.2f}  {rec[c]:6.2f}  {f1[c]:5.2f}  {mcc_c:6.2f}")
print(f"\nmulti-class MCC: {matthews_corrcoef(y_te, test_pred):.3f}  (scikit-learn uses the multiclass generalization of the binary formula)")

ROC curve. A classifier that outputs a score needs a threshold to turn it into yes/no. Sliding the threshold trades false positives against false negatives; the ROC curve plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate for every threshold. Below: the “cross” perceptron’s score, cross vs. everything else. AUROC is 0.5 for random guessing and 1.0 for a perfect ranking.

c = PAT_NAMES.index("cross")
fpr, tpr, thr = roc_curve(y_te == c, scores(W_pat, X_te)[:, c])
auc_cross = roc_auc_score(y_te == c, scores(W_pat, X_te)[:, c])

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
im = a1.imshow(cm, cmap="Blues")
a1.set_xticks(range(5)); a1.set_xticklabels(PAT_NAMES, rotation=40, ha="right")
a1.set_yticks(range(5)); a1.set_yticklabels(PAT_NAMES)
for i in range(5):
    for j in range(5):
        a1.text(j, i, cm[i, j], ha="center", va="center", color="white" if cm[i, j] > 20 else "black")
a1.set_xlabel("predicted"); a1.set_ylabel("true")
a1.set_title(f"Test-set confusion matrix (accuracy {(test_pred == y_te).mean():.2f})")
a2.plot(fpr, tpr, color="#d9822b", lw=2, label=f"'cross' perceptron (AUROC = {auc_cross:.2f})")
a2.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", color="grey", label="random (AUROC = 0.5)")
a2.set_xlabel("false-positive rate"); a2.set_ylabel("true-positive rate")
a2.set_title("ROC curve: cross vs. rest"); a2.legend(loc="lower right")

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
text:
Evaluating a regression model
Regression predictions are not right or wrong, only more or less off. The standard numbers, computed on held-out proteins from the helix example:

RMSE \(=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}\), in the target’s own units;
Pearson \(r\) between predicted and true values;
\(R^2\) \(= 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{\sum (y_i-\bar y)^2}\), the fraction of variance explained (0 = no better than predicting the mean).

They answer different questions. RMSE: how far off are the predictions, in the target’s units? \(r\): do the predictions follow the ups and downs of the truth? \(R^2\): how much better are they than always predicting the mean?

xh_tr, xh_te, yh_tr, yh_te = train_test_split(former_frac.reshape(-1, 1), helix_frac, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
lin = LinearRegression().fit(xh_tr, yh_tr)
pred_te = lin.predict(xh_te)
rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yh_te, pred_te))
baseline_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yh_te, np.full_like(yh_te, yh_tr.mean())))
print(f"{len(yh_tr)} training / {len(yh_te)} test proteins")
print(f"test RMSE: {rmse:.3f}   (predicting the training mean for everything: {baseline_rmse:.3f})")
print(f"test Pearson r: {pearsonr(yh_te, pred_te)[0]:.3f}")
print(f"test R^2: {r2_score(yh_te, pred_te):.3f}")

41 training / 14 test proteins
test RMSE: 0.159   (predicting the training mean for everything: 0.234)
test Pearson r: 0.760
test R^2: 0.526


A high correlation is not the same as accurate predictions. Stretch and shift the same predictions, \(\hat y' = 2\hat y + 0.3\), as a systematically biased predictor would: the ordering is untouched, so \(r\) stays exactly the same, but the numbers are now far off.

biased = 2 * pred_te + 0.3
print(f"biased predictions:  Pearson r = {pearsonr(yh_te, biased)[0]:.3f}   "
      f"RMSE = {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yh_te, biased)):.3f}   R^2 = {r2_score(yh_te, biased):.3f}")

biased predictions:  Pearson r = 0.760   RMSE = 0.639   R^2 = -6.670


Why the test set matters, in one picture. A model that is flexible enough can simply memorize its training data. 1-nearest-neighbour is the extreme case: it predicts the helix fraction of the most similar protein (by amino-acid composition) that it was trained on. Evaluated on the proteins it was trained on, every protein’s nearest neighbour is itself, so the predictions are perfect. On held-out proteins it is no better than predicting the mean.

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

# A model flexible enough to memorize: 1-nearest-neighbour on the 20 amino-acid fractions.
# It predicts the helix fraction of the most similar protein it was trained on.
AAS = "ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY"
comp = np.array([[s.count(a) / len(s) for a in AAS] for s in helix_seqs])
idx_tr, idx_te = train_test_split(np.arange(len(helix_frac)), test_size=0.25, random_state=0)   # the same split as above

knn_all = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=1).fit(comp, helix_frac)         # trained on ALL 55 proteins ...
pred_all = knn_all.predict(comp)                                           # ... and evaluated on the same 55
knn = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=1).fit(comp[idx_tr], helix_frac[idx_tr])
pred_knn_te = knn.predict(comp[idx_te])

def report(name, y, p):
    print(f"{name:52s} RMSE {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y, p)):.3f}   r {pearsonr(y, p)[0]:.3f}   R^2 {r2_score(y, p):.3f}")
report("linear, 1 feature, 14 held-out proteins", yh_te, pred_te)
report("1-nearest-neighbour, trained and evaluated on all 55", helix_frac, pred_all)
report("1-nearest-neighbour, 14 held-out proteins", helix_frac[idx_te], pred_knn_te)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.3), sharex=True, sharey=True)
panels = [(axes[0], lin.predict(xh_tr), yh_tr, pred_te, yh_te, "Linear model (1 feature)\nheld-out proteins"),
          (axes[1], None, None, pred_all, helix_frac, "1-nearest-neighbour\nevaluated on its own training data"),
          (axes[2], knn.predict(comp[idx_tr]), helix_frac[idx_tr], pred_knn_te, helix_frac[idx_te],
           "1-nearest-neighbour\nheld-out proteins")]
for ax, p_tr, y_tr_, p, y, title in panels:
    if p_tr is not None:
        ax.scatter(y_tr_, p_tr, s=14, color="lightgrey", label="training proteins")
    ax.scatter(y, p, s=28, color="tab:blue" if "held-out" in title else "tab:red",
               label="held-out proteins" if "held-out" in title else "the same 55 proteins")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nR² = {r2_score(y, p):.2f}, RMSE = {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y, p)):.2f}", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("measured helix fraction")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("predicted helix fraction")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(f"{FIGS}/session08-regression-evaluation.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

text:
Real data: the subcellular-localization dataset
Mitochondrion is the smallest class. First, a look at what class imbalance does to accuracy, using the unambiguous entries we fetched, without balancing. Note that we asked UniProt for only the first 500 hits per class, to keep the download small. The real class sizes are 864, 1316, 220, 924 and 1146, so the cap understates the imbalance:

counts = np.array([len(entries_by_class[c]) for c in CLASS_NAMES])
y_all = np.repeat(np.arange(5), counts)
majority = counts.argmax()
always_majority = np.full_like(y_all, majority)
print("class sizes:", dict(zip(CLASS_NAMES, counts.tolist())))
print(f"'always predict {CLASS_NAMES[majority]}': accuracy = {(always_majority == y_all).mean():.3f}, "
      f"MCC = {matthews_corrcoef(y_all, always_majority):.3f}")
print(f"'always predict Mitochondrion': accuracy = {(y_all == 2).mean():.3f}")

'always predict Nucleus': accuracy = 0.263, MCC = 0.000
'always predict Mitochondrion': accuracy = 0.074


A classifier that has learned nothing still scores well above the 20% you might expect for five classes, while MCC correctly reports 0. From here on the classes are balanced to the size of the smallest one:

N_PER_CLASS = counts.min()
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
balanced_accs, balanced_seqs, balanced_labels = [], [], []
for class_idx, class_name in enumerate(CLASS_NAMES):
    pool = entries_by_class[class_name]
    for i in rng.choice(len(pool), N_PER_CLASS, replace=False):
        balanced_accs.append(pool[i][0])
        balanced_seqs.append(pool[i][1])
        balanced_labels.append(class_idx)
print("balanced dataset:", len(balanced_seqs), "sequences,", N_PER_CLASS, "per class")

AMINO_ACIDS = "ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY"
AA_TO_INDEX = {aa: i for i, aa in enumerate(AMINO_ACIDS)}
SEQ_LEN = 150   # localization signals are mostly N-terminal

def one_hot_encode(sequence, length=SEQ_LEN):
    encoded = np.zeros((length, len(AMINO_ACIDS)), dtype=np.float32)
    for position, residue in enumerate(sequence[:length]):
        if residue in AA_TO_INDEX:
            encoded[position, AA_TO_INDEX[residue]] = 1.0
    return encoded.flatten()

X = np.stack([one_hot_encode(s) for s in balanced_seqs])
y = np.array(balanced_labels)
print("X shape:", X.shape, " (sequences x 150 positions x 20 amino acids, flattened)")

balanced dataset: 700 sequences, 140 per class
X shape: (700, 3000)  (sequences x 150 positions x 20 amino acids, flattened)



How much can you trust a single split?
A fast baseline (logistic regression on the one-hot features), refitted on ten different random stratified 70/15/15 splits:

idx_all = np.arange(len(y))
random_split_acc = []
for seed in range(10):
    tr, tmp = train_test_split(idx_all, test_size=0.30, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
    va, te = train_test_split(tmp, test_size=0.5, stratify=y[tmp], random_state=seed)
    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=0).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
    random_split_acc.append(clf.score(X[va], y[va]))
random_split_acc = np.array(random_split_acc)
print("validation accuracy per split:", np.round(random_split_acc, 3))
print(f"mean = {random_split_acc.mean():.3f}, std = {random_split_acc.std():.3f}, "
      f"range = [{random_split_acc.min():.3f}, {random_split_acc.max():.3f}]")

validation accuracy per split: [0.581 0.571 0.552 0.6   0.571 0.505 0.533 0.552 0.61  0.533]
mean = 0.561, std = 0.031, range = [0.505, 0.610]




Cross-validation
k-fold cross-validation uses every example for validation exactly once: split into \(k\) stratified folds, train on \(k-1\), validate on the remaining one, and average. It makes better use of limited data and reduces the dependence on one particular split; it does not remove sampling variability (the folds are still one sample of proteins).

kfold = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
fold_acc = []
for fold, (tr, va) in enumerate(kfold.split(X, y)):
    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=0).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
    fold_acc.append(clf.score(X[va], y[va]))
    print(f"fold {fold}: {len(tr)} train / {len(va)} val -> accuracy {fold_acc[-1]:.3f}")
print(f"5-fold CV: mean = {np.mean(fold_acc):.3f}, std = {np.std(fold_acc):.3f}")

fold 0: 560 train / 140 val -> accuracy 0.600
fold 1: 560 train / 140 val -> accuracy 0.471
fold 2: 560 train / 140 val -> accuracy 0.571
fold 3: 560 train / 140 val -> accuracy 0.536
fold 4: 560 train / 140 val -> accuracy 0.521
5-fold CV: mean = 0.540, std = 0.044

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
section: The biological trap: homologs on both sides of the split
text:
The biological trap: homologs on both sides of the split
A random split treats every protein as independent. Proteins are not independent: they come in families of homologs (Session 4) that share sequence and usually function and localization. If one family member is in the training set and another in the test set, the model can exploit family-specific sequence similarity rather than relying only on general localization signals. The test then partly measures recognition of known families rather than generalisation to new kinds of proteins.
The standard remedy is homology partitioning: cluster the sequences by identity, then assign whole clusters to training, validation or test, so that no cluster crosses the split. This substantially reduces homology leakage; it does not remove every remote homolog below the identity cutoff. Here we cluster at 30% identity with MMseqs2 (a fast alternative to all-against-all BLAST). If mmseqs isn’t installed (e.g. on Colab), the notebook loads the precomputed clustering of the same 700 proteins from the course repository.

CLUSTER_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/main/notebooks/data/session08-subcell-mmseqs-30.tsv"
LOCAL_TSV = "data/session08-subcell-mmseqs-30.tsv"

def mmseqs_clusters(accs, seqs, min_seq_id=0.3):
    tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    with open(f"{tmp}/in.fasta", "w") as f:
        for a, s in zip(accs, seqs):
            f.write(f">{a}\n{s}\n")
    subprocess.run(["mmseqs", "easy-cluster", f"{tmp}/in.fasta", f"{tmp}/clu", f"{tmp}/work",
                    "--min-seq-id", str(min_seq_id), "-c", "0.5", "-v", "1"],
                   check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    pairs = [line.split("\t") for line in open(f"{tmp}/clu_cluster.tsv").read().split("\n") if line]
    shutil.rmtree(tmp)
    return {member: rep for rep, member in pairs}

def load_precomputed_clusters():
    text = open(LOCAL_TSV).read() if os.path.exists(LOCAL_TSV) else requests.get(CLUSTER_URL, timeout=30).text
    pairs = [line.split("\t") for line in text.strip().split("\n")[1:]]
    return {member: rep for rep, member in pairs}

if shutil.which("mmseqs"):
    member_to_rep = mmseqs_clusters(balanced_accs, balanced_seqs)
    print("clustered with local MMseqs2 (30% identity, 50% coverage)")
else:
    member_to_rep = load_precomputed_clusters()
    print("mmseqs not found -- loaded the precomputed MMseqs2 clustering")

# proteins missing from the clustering (e.g. if UniProt changed) become their own cluster
reps = [member_to_rep.get(a, a) for a in balanced_accs]
rep_ids = {r: i for i, r in enumerate(sorted(set(reps)))}
groups = np.array([rep_ids[r] for r in reps])
sizes = np.bincount(groups)
print(f"{len(y)} proteins -> {len(sizes)} clusters; "
      f"{(sizes > 1).sum()} clusters have more than one member ({sizes[sizes > 1].sum()} proteins), largest has {sizes.max()}")

clustered with local MMseqs2 (30% identity, 50% coverage)
700 proteins -> 551 clusters; 75 clusters have more than one member (224 proteins), largest has 11


How often does a random split put a protein’s homolog in the training set, and what does that do to the baseline’s accuracy? We pool the validation predictions from the same ten random splits as above:

with_homolog, without_homolog, leak_frac = [], [], []
for seed in range(10):
    tr, tmp = train_test_split(idx_all, test_size=0.30, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
    va, te = train_test_split(tmp, test_size=0.5, stratify=y[tmp], random_state=seed)
    pred = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=0).fit(X[tr], y[tr]).predict(X[va])
    train_groups = set(groups[tr])
    has = np.array([groups[i] in train_groups for i in va])
    leak_frac.append(has.mean())
    with_homolog += list(pred[has] == y[va][has])
    without_homolog += list(pred[~has] == y[va][~has])
print(f"validation proteins with a >=30%-identity homolog in the training set: {np.mean(leak_frac):.1%}")
print(f"accuracy on those:      {np.mean(with_homolog):.3f}  (n = {len(with_homolog)})")
print(f"accuracy on the rest:   {np.mean(without_homolog):.3f}  (n = {len(without_homolog)})")

validation proteins with a >=30%-identity homolog in the training set: 31.3%
accuracy on those:      0.675  (n = 329)
accuracy on the rest:   0.509  (n = 721)


Now a homology-aware split: clusters are assigned whole, one at a time in random order, to whichever of train/validation/test is furthest below its 70/15/15 share of that cluster’s classes. No cluster crosses the split. The function is deterministic and uses plain NumPy, so Sessions 9 and 10 can copy it and get exactly the same split.

def homology_split(y, groups, fractions=(0.70, 0.15, 0.15), seed=0):
    '''Assign whole clusters, in random order, to train/val/test: each cluster
    goes to the split furthest below its target share of that cluster's
    classes (ties broken at random). Returns three index arrays.'''
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    n_classes = y.max() + 1
    target = np.outer(fractions, np.bincount(y, minlength=n_classes))   # (3 splits, n_classes)
    have = np.zeros_like(target)
    assignment = {}
    for g in rng.permutation(np.unique(groups)):
        cls_counts = np.bincount(y[groups == g], minlength=n_classes)
        deficit = ((target - have) * (cls_counts > 0)).sum(axis=1) / target.sum(axis=1)
        best = np.flatnonzero(deficit == deficit.max())
        split = int(rng.choice(best))
        assignment[g] = split
        have[split] += cls_counts
    split_of = np.array([assignment[g] for g in groups])
    return [np.where(split_of == k)[0] for k in range(3)]

tr_h, va_h, te_h = homology_split(y, groups)
assert not (set(groups[tr_h]) & set(groups[va_h]) or set(groups[tr_h]) & set(groups[te_h]) or set(groups[va_h]) & set(groups[te_h]))
print(f"homology-aware split: train {len(tr_h)} / val {len(va_h)} / test {len(te_h)}")
for name, ix in [("train", tr_h), ("val", va_h), ("test", te_h)]:
    print(f"  {name:5s} per class: {np.bincount(y[ix], minlength=5).tolist()}")

homology-aware split: train 486 / val 105 / test 109
  train per class: [98, 98, 98, 94, 98]
  val   per class: [21, 21, 21, 21, 21]
  test  per class: [21, 21, 21, 25, 21]


Is the baseline worse on homology-aware splits? One split is too noisy to tell (the std across random splits above is about 0.03), so compare ten of each, pooling validation and test accuracy:

def baseline_acc(tr, va, te):
    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=0).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
    return (clf.score(X[va], y[va]) + clf.score(X[te], y[te])) / 2

random_acc, homology_acc = [], []
for seed in range(10):
    tr, tmp = train_test_split(idx_all, test_size=0.30, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
    va, te = train_test_split(tmp, test_size=0.5, stratify=y[tmp], random_state=seed)
    random_acc.append(baseline_acc(tr, va, te))
    homology_acc.append(baseline_acc(*homology_split(y, groups, seed=seed)))
print(f"random splits:          mean accuracy {np.mean(random_acc):.3f}  (std {np.std(random_acc):.3f})")
print(f"homology-aware splits:  mean accuracy {np.mean(homology_acc):.3f}  (std {np.std(homology_acc):.3f})")

random splits:          mean accuracy 0.553  (std 0.019)
homology-aware splits:  mean accuracy 0.536  (std 0.026)



# Figure 1: how much one split varies, and 5-fold cross-validation
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
jit = np.random.RandomState(0).uniform(-0.08, 0.08, 10)
ax.scatter(random_split_acc, 1 + jit, color="tab:blue", s=40, label="10 random 70/15/15 splits (validation)")
ax.scatter(fold_acc, 0 + jit[:len(fold_acc)], color="tab:orange", s=40, label="5 folds of one cross-validation")
ax.errorbar(np.mean(fold_acc), -0.35, xerr=np.std(fold_acc), fmt="D", color="tab:orange", capsize=4,
            label=f"cross-validation mean ± std ({np.mean(fold_acc):.3f})")
ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticklabels(["CV folds", "random splits"]); ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("accuracy of the logistic-regression baseline")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.28), ncol=2, frameon=False)
ax.set_title("Same data, same model: the split alone moves accuracy by ±0.05")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(f"{FIGS}/session08-split-noise.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

# Figure 2: homology leakage
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
vals = [np.mean(with_homolog), np.mean(without_homolog)]
axes[0].bar(["homolog in training\n(n = %d)" % len(with_homolog), "no homolog in training\n(n = %d)" % len(without_homolog)],
            vals, color=["tab:red", "tab:blue"])
for k, v in enumerate(vals):
    axes[0].text(k, v + 0.01, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center")
axes[0].axhline(0.2, color="grey", ls=":", label="chance (5 classes)")
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 0.8); axes[0].set_ylabel("accuracy of the baseline"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title(f"Random splits: {np.mean(leak_frac):.1%} of validation proteins\nhave a ≥30%-identity homolog in training", fontsize=10)
for k, (accs, name, col) in enumerate([(random_acc, "random splits", "tab:red"), (homology_acc, "homology-aware splits", "tab:blue")]):
    axes[1].scatter(np.full(len(accs), k) + jit, accs, color=col, s=40)
    axes[1].plot([k - 0.2, k + 0.2], [np.mean(accs)] * 2, color="k", lw=2)
    axes[1].text(k + 0.25, np.mean(accs), f"mean {np.mean(accs):.3f}", va="center", fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_xticks([0, 1]); axes[1].set_xticklabels(["random splits", "homology-aware splits"])
axes[1].set_xlim(-0.5, 1.8); axes[1].set_ylabel("accuracy (validation + test)")
axes[1].set_title("Ten splits of each kind", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(f"{FIGS}/session08-homology-leakage.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()















The overall drop is small here, because 476 of the 700 proteins (the singleton clusters) have no homolog in the dataset at all. What matters is the per-protein effect above: a protein with a homolog in training is classified correctly far more often. In more redundant datasets (a whole proteome, or the PDB, where some families have thousands of members) the gap between random and homology-aware evaluation becomes much larger.
This homology-aware split is the one used from here on, and by Session 9 and Session 10’s notebooks. Numbers measured on it are lower, and more honest.

X_train, y_train = X[tr_h], y[tr_h]
X_val, y_val = X[va_h], y[va_h]
X_test, y_test = X[te_h], y[te_h]
print(f"train: {len(X_train)}   val: {len(X_val)}   test: {len(X_test)}")

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
section: From step functions to trainable activations
text:
From step functions to trainable activations
Session 7’s perceptron used a step function. Its derivative is zero almost everywhere, which gives gradient descent nothing to follow. Networks replace it with functions that have a useful gradient. Sigmoid and tanh are smooth; ReLU has a kink at zero, but its slope is 1 or 0 everywhere else, which is enough for gradient descent. You have already met the sigmoid in Part 1.
\[
\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} \qquad \tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z) - 1 \qquad \text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)
\]
(Their derivatives, and why that matters for deep networks, are Session 9’s topic.)

def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))
def relu(x): return np.maximum(0, x)

x = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.plot(x, np.where(x > 0, 1.0, 0.0), color="grey", lw=1, ls="--", label="step (Session 7)")
plt.plot(x, sigmoid(x), label="sigmoid")
plt.plot(x, np.tanh(x), label="tanh")
plt.plot(x, relu(x), label="ReLU")
plt.axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.5)
plt.axvline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.5)
plt.ylim(-1.2, 3)
plt.legend()
plt.title("The step function and three trainable replacements")
plt.xlabel("z"); plt.ylabel("activation(z)")
plt.savefig(f"{FIGS}/session08-activation-functions.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
section: From one output to many: softmax
text:
From one output to many: softmax
The 3×3 classifier produces five scores and picks the largest. Softmax turns \(K\) scores (logits) into \(K\) positive numbers that sum to 1:
\[
\text{softmax}(z)_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}}
\]
Applied to the five perceptron scores for one noisy test pattern:

i = int(np.where((test_pred != y_te))[0][0])     # the first misclassified test example
z = scores(W_pat, X_te[i:i+1])[0]
p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
print(f"true class: {PAT_NAMES[y_te[i]]}")
print(f"{'class':>14s}  {'score z':>8s}  {'softmax':>8s}")
for name, zi, pi in zip(PAT_NAMES, z, p):
    print(f"{name:>14s}  {zi:8.2f}  {pi:8.3f}")
print("sum of the softmax values:", round(p.sum(), 6))

true class: horizontal
         class   score z   softmax
    horizontal     -2.19     0.059
      vertical     -0.80     0.235
      diagonal     -2.35     0.050
 anti-diagonal     -2.61     0.039
         cross      0.16     0.618
sum of the softmax values: 1.0


Softmax never changes which class wins. It expresses the relative scores as a normalized distribution. These perceptron scores were never trained with cross-entropy, so the numbers sum to 1 but should not be read as reliable probabilities. Training with cross-entropy (Session 9) makes them more interpretable, but it does not by itself guarantee that they are calibrated (that a predicted 0.8 is right 80% of the time); that has to be checked on held-out data.

title: Session 8 — Machine Learning Foundations & Practical PyTorch, in code
text:
Practical PyTorch: models as classes
A PyTorch model is a class inheriting from nn.Module: its layers are attributes created in __init__, and forward() says how input becomes output. The 3×3 classifier is exactly one nn.Linear(9, 5) layer. Copying the perceptron weights into it gives identical predictions:

class PatternClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(9, 5)      # 5 outputs, each a weighted sum of 9 pixels + bias

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.linear(x)              # raw scores (logits)

pat_model = PatternClassifier()
with torch.no_grad():
    pat_model.linear.bias.copy_(torch.tensor(W_pat[:, 0]))
    pat_model.linear.weight.copy_(torch.tensor(W_pat[:, 1:]))
    torch_pred = pat_model(torch.tensor(X_te, dtype=torch.float32)).argmax(dim=1).numpy()
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in pat_model.parameters()), "(5 x 9 weights + 5 biases)")
print("identical predictions to the NumPy perceptrons:", bool((torch_pred == test_pred).all()))

parameters: 50 (5 x 9 weights + 5 biases)
identical predictions to the NumPy perceptrons: True



The localization network, defined but not trained
The same pattern, bigger: 3000 inputs, one hidden layer of 64 ReLU units, and 5 output logits. There is no softmax layer: Session 9’s nn.CrossEntropyLoss combines log-softmax with the negative log-likelihood in one numerically stable operation, so the model should output raw logits.

class SubcellularLocalizationClassifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim=SEQ_LEN * len(AMINO_ACIDS), hidden_dim=64, n_classes=5, dropout=0.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(dropout),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, n_classes),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)  # raw logits, shape (batch, n_classes)


model = SubcellularLocalizationClassifier()
print(model)
print("total trainable parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))

SubcellularLocalizationClassifier(
  (net): Sequential(
    (0): Linear(in_features=3000, out_features=64, bias=True)
    (1): ReLU()
    (2): Dropout(p=0.0, inplace=False)
    (3): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=5, bias=True)
  )
)
total trainable parameters: 192389


One forward pass on the validation set checks that the shapes work. The weights are still random. The metrics show what “no better than chance” looks like, and give the baseline Session 9 compares against.

X_val_t = torch.tensor(X_val, dtype=torch.float32)
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(X_val_t)
print("input shape: ", tuple(X_val_t.shape))
print("output shape:", tuple(logits.shape))

predicted = logits.argmax(dim=1).numpy()
probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1).numpy()
_, _, f1_macro, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(y_val, predicted, average="macro", zero_division=0)
print(f"\naccuracy:    {(predicted == y_val).mean():.3f}   (chance: 0.20)")
print(f"F1:          {f1_macro:.3f}")
print(f"MCC:         {matthews_corrcoef(y_val, predicted):.3f}")
print(f"AUROC:       {roc_auc_score(y_val, probs, multi_class='ovr'):.3f}")
print("confusion matrix:\n", confusion_matrix(y_val, predicted))

Try it yourself

Change SIGMA in the 3×3 section (e.g. 0.5 or 1.2), re-run, and watch test accuracy and the confusion matrix. Which pairs of patterns get confused, and why?

title: 9  Session 9: How a Neural Network Learns, and Why Training Fails
text:
9.1 Learning goals
By the end of this session you should be able to:
Sessions 7, 8 and 9 form one progression. Session 7 asked what a neural network can represent. Session 8 asked how we know whether a model generalises. This session asks how we actually train a network, and why training sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails.
The starting point is concrete. In Session 8 we built a network, but its weights were random, so its predictions were no better than chance. We had labelled examples, so how do we turn the random weights into useful predictions? This session answers that question with four datasets. Breast-cancer biopsies introduce the training loop, and a protein fitness landscape shows why training fails and when a hidden layer pays off. Session 8’s protein localisation data show what happens when a network is too large for its data, and blood-cell images are used in the lab.

section: 9.2 From an untrained network to a trained network
text:
9.2 From an untrained network to a trained network
We start with a problem on which training works well. The Wisconsin breast-cancer dataset has 569 fine-needle biopsies, each described by 30 features measured on microscope images of the cell nuclei (radius, texture, perimeter, smoothness, concavity and so on). Each biopsy is labelled malignant (212) or benign (357). We split the data into 398 training, 85 validation and 86 test biopsies, and standardise the features with statistics from the training set only (Session 8). Table 9.1 summarises the data.



Table 9.1: The breast-cancer data.









Examples
569 fine-needle biopsies of breast lumps


Label
malignant (212) or benign (357)


Features
30: ten measurements of the cell nuclei in the image (radius, texture, perimeter, area, smoothness, compactness, concavity, concave points, symmetry, fractal dimension), each given as the mean, the standard error and the worst (largest) value over the nuclei


Split
training 398 (148 malignant), validation 85 (32), test 86 (32); stratified, so each set has the same share of malignant biopsies


Preprocessing
each feature standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, with the mean and standard deviation of the training set






Some features separate the two classes well on their own, others hardly at all (Figure 9.1):






Figure 9.1: Four of the 30 features (the mean value over the nuclei), benign against malignant biopsies, with each feature’s AUROC on its own (Session 8). Malignant nuclei are larger and have more concave points; texture helps a little, and fractal dimension not at all (an AUROC of 0.5 is guessing).



The network reads all 30 standardised features at once. It has one hidden layer of 16 ReLU units and one output unit, whose sigmoid gives the probability that the biopsy is malignant (Figure 9.2). Counting the biases, it has 513 weights to learn.






Figure 9.2: The breast-cancer network. Every input feature is connected to every hidden unit, and every hidden unit to the output (only some of the 30 inputs and 16 hidden units are drawn). The output is a logit; the sigmoid turns it into P(malignant), and the loss function BCEWithLogitsLoss applies the sigmoid itself.



Training the network means repeating one cycle over and over:






Figure 9.3: The training cycle. The network turns inputs into predictions; the loss measures how wrong they are compared with the labels; backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight; the optimiser updates the weights. The same five lines of PyTorch (right) do this for every mini-batch, in every epoch.



Before training, the network’s predicted probabilities all sit close to 0.5, so the network is guessing (validation accuracy 0.659, roughly the share of benign biopsies). After 100 passes through the training data, the benign biopsies are pushed towards 0 and the malignant ones towards 1:






Figure 9.4: Left: training and validation loss per epoch. Both fall quickly; after about 50 epochs the validation loss stops improving while the training loss keeps falling, and we keep the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss (early stopping). Right: predicted probability of malignancy for the 85 validation biopsies, before and after training.



On the test set the trained network reaches an accuracy of 0.953, an MCC of 0.900 and an AUROC of 0.984. Only 2 benign biopsies are called malignant, and only 2 malignant ones are missed.
Was the hidden layer needed? Not here. We compare the models by 5-fold cross-validation, because a single test split of 86 biopsies is too noisy for this comparison (Session 8). Logistic regression with 31 weights and the network with 513 both reach an accuracy of 0.979. Malignant and benign nuclei differ mainly in size and shape, and a weighted sum of those measurements already separates them. Training therefore works, but the extra capacity has nothing to add. Section 9.6 shows a dataset where it does.

title: 9  Session 9: How a Neural Network Learns, and Why Training Fails
text:
9.3 How backpropagation finds every gradient
Gradient descent (Session 1, Session 7) needs \(\partial L / \partial w\), the slope of the loss, for every weight. For a single layer that was easy. But what about a weight buried several layers inside a network, whose effect on the loss passes through every later layer? The tiny network below shows how backpropagation answers this question.






Figure 9.5: A tiny network: two inputs, one tanh hidden unit \(h\), one sigmoid output \(\hat y\), and the loss \(L\). The forward pass (grey) computes the prediction and the loss. The backward pass (red) applies the chain rule from the loss back towards the inputs: \(\partial L/\partial \hat y\) is computed once and reused for \(w_3\), then multiplied by \(\partial \hat y/\partial h\) and reused for \(w_1\) and \(w_2\).



For \(w_1\), the chain rule multiplies the local slopes along the path from the loss back to the weight:
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat y}\;\frac{\partial \hat y}{\partial h}\;\frac{\partial h}{\partial w_1}
\]
Backpropagation is an efficient application of the chain rule, from the loss backwards through the network. Each layer’s “error signal” is computed once and reused for all the weights feeding into it, so computing all the gradients costs about as much as one forward pass. Without that reuse, networks with thousands or millions of weights could not be trained.
In practice, you do not have to differentiate networks by hand. The notebook does it once for the tiny network above, working out the five gradients with the chain rule. It then builds the same network in PyTorch and calls loss.backward(), and all five gradients agree to eight decimal places. From then on, PyTorch’s autograd does the work for any network.
Putting these pieces together gives the training loop that you will write yourself in the lab:
for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    for xb, yb in loader:                 # one mini-batch at a time
        optimizer.zero_grad()             # 1. clear the old gradients
        logits = model(xb)                # 2. forward pass
        loss = criterion(logits, yb)      # 3. how wrong is it?
        loss.backward()                   # 4. backpropagation: every gradient
        optimizer.step()                  # 5. update every weight
Real training uses mini-batches. A DataLoader shuffles the training set every epoch and serves it in small batches (here 32 biopsies), and the weights are updated after every batch. Each epoch (one pass through the training data) therefore consists of many cheap, slightly noisy steps instead of one expensive exact step. This is stochastic gradient descent. After every epoch we measure the validation loss and keep the best weights (early stopping).

9.3.1 Further watching
Backpropagation, intuitively (3Blue1Brown, Deep Learning ch. 3): the same chain-rule idea as above, built up visually one layer at a time. (Chapter 1, But what is a neural network?, is embedded on Session 7.)



Optional video: Backpropagation calculus (3Blue1Brown, Deep Learning ch. 4, 10 min), the full chain-rule mechanics for a general multi-layer network.

title: 9  Session 9: How a Neural Network Learns, and Why Training Fails
text:
9.4 Which loss to minimise
The training loop minimises a loss, and the loss decides what “wrong” means. For regression we use the mean squared error between prediction and target. For classification we use cross-entropy, which for one example is the negative log of the probability that the model gave the true class,
\[
\text{CE} = -\log p(\text{true class}),
\]
that is, its surprise in the language of Session 1. Averaged over a dataset, cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood, so minimising it is the same as maximum likelihood (Session 1).






Figure 9.6: Cross-entropy as a function of the probability given to the true class. A confident correct answer costs almost nothing; a confident mistake costs a lot.



Cross-entropy punishes a confident mistake far more than hedging. A probability of 0.9 on the true class costs 0.105, but a probability of 0.01 costs 4.6, over 40 times more. This is what pushes a classifier to separate the classes, as in the right panel of the breast-cancer figure. In PyTorch, nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss (for two classes) and nn.CrossEntropyLoss (for more classes) combine the sigmoid or log-softmax with this loss in one numerically stable step, so the model outputs raw logits (Session 8). The notebook checks both by hand. The lab compares cross-entropy with the mean squared and mean absolute error for the same blood-cell classifier, and cross-entropy trains best.






NoteOptional: cross-entropy and relative entropy





Cross-entropy is built from the relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence) of Session 4. It is the entropy of the true distribution plus the extra cost of describing it with the model’s distribution \(Q\): \(H(P, Q) = H(P) + D_{\text{KL}}(P \| Q)\). Since \(H(P)\) does not depend on the model, minimising cross-entropy is the same as minimising the KL divergence between the model’s predictions and the true labels.



Optional video: But what is cross-entropy? (3Blue1Brown, Compression is Intelligence part 2, 34 min), cross-entropy from the information-theory side, built up from first principles.

title: 9  Session 9: How a Neural Network Learns, and Why Training Fails
text:
9.5 Why training fails
The training loop always runs, but it does not always learn. This section shows three common failures. Each is produced by changing one thing in a network that predicts the fitness of protein variants, using the GB1 data of Section 9.6 (20,000 training variants, each described by the one-hot encoding of four residues). We measure the validation error as the mean absolute error (MAE) of the predicted \(\log_{10}\) fitness. As reference points, predicting the training mean for every variant gives an MAE of 0.488, and a working 64/64 network reaches 0.250 within 20 epochs.






NoteThe GB1 data in brief



The full story is in Section 9.6; this is what you need for this section.







Protein
GB1, a small antibody-binding (IgG) domain of the bacterial protein G


Variants
all 20⁴ = 160,000 combinations of amino acids at four positions (V39, D40, G41, V54); 149,361 have a measured value (Wu et al., 2016)


Label (regression)
how well the variant binds IgG, relative to the wild type VDGV (= 1), as \(\log_{10}(\text{fitness} + 0.001)\)


Input
the one-hot encoding of the four residues (Session 7): 4 × 20 = 80 numbers


Split
20,000 variants for training, 5,000 for validation, 20,000 for testing


Network
“64/64”: two hidden layers of 64 units each and one output, 9,409 weights


Reference points (validation MAE)
0.488 predicting the training mean; 0.371 the additive (linear) model; 0.250 the working 64/64 network











Figure 9.7: Four experiments. (1) Gradient size per layer in a freshly initialised network with six hidden layers: with sigmoid, the first layer receives about ten million times less gradient than the last. (2) Starting every weight at the same value. (3) Six hidden layers with sigmoid, tanh or ReLU, trained with plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and sigmoid trained with Adam. (4) Optimiser and learning rate. The dotted line is the error of predicting the mean.




9.5.1 Failure 1: every weight starts the same

Observation. Start all weights at 0.1 instead of small random numbers. After 20 epochs the validation MAE is 0.352, little better than the additive (linear) model’s 0.371, against 0.250 from a random start.
Why? Every hidden unit computes the same thing and receives the same gradient, so the units stay identical for ever. After training, all 64 units in the first layer are still exactly the same, so 64 units behave like one.
Fix. Random initialisation breaks the symmetry, and PyTorch does this by default.



9.5.2 Failure 2: deep sigmoid networks, and vanishing gradients

Observation. A network with six hidden layers of sigmoid units, trained with plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD), does not learn at all. Its validation MAE stays around 0.48, the error of predicting the mean. The same network with tanh (0.321) or ReLU (0.312) does learn.
Why? The answer lies in the activation functions and the chain rule, explained below.

The chain rule, one layer at a time. In Section 9.3, the gradient for a weight was a product of local slopes along the path from the loss back to that weight. In a deep network, this path passes through every later layer. To see what happens, take the simplest deep network: one unit per layer, six hidden layers. Unit \(k\) computes \(z_k = w_k h_{k-1}\) and passes on \(h_k = f(z_k)\), where \(f\) is the activation function and \(h_0 = x\) is the input. The gradient for the first weight is then
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_6}\;
\underbrace{f'(z_6)\,w_6}_{\text{layer 6}}\;
\underbrace{f'(z_5)\,w_5}_{\text{layer 5}}\;\cdots\;
\underbrace{f'(z_2)\,w_2}_{\text{layer 2}}\;
f'(z_1)\,x .
\]
Each layer that the gradient passes through on its way back contributes two factors: its weight \(w_k\) and the slope of its activation function at that unit’s weighted sum, \(f'(z_k)\). In a real network each layer has many units and the gradient is a sum over many such paths, but every path is a product of this kind. A product of many numbers smaller than 1 shrinks exponentially with its length. The size of those slopes therefore decides whether a gradient survives the trip back (Figure 9.8):

Sigmoid. Its slope is at most 0.25, at \(z = 0\), and falls quickly on both sides (about 0.20 at \(|z| = 1\) and below 0.01 at \(|z| = 6\)). Even in the best case, six layers therefore multiply the gradient by \(0.25^6 \approx 0.00024\); with units away from \(z = 0\), it shrinks even faster.
Tanh. Its slope is 1 at \(z = 0\), four times larger than sigmoid’s, so the gradient shrinks more slowly. But it still falls in both tails (0.42 at \(|z| = 1\)), so units that are far from zero still block the gradient.
ReLU. Its slope is exactly 1 for every unit that is active (\(z > 0\)), so the activation does not shrink the gradient at all along active paths. For inactive units it is exactly 0, and those paths carry no gradient.

The weights \(w_k\) in the product matter as well. Large weights can make the gradient explode instead, which is why initialisation scales them to each layer’s size. Measured in the freshly initialised network, the first layer’s gradient is about ten million times smaller than the last layer’s with sigmoid, against a few hundred to two thousand times smaller with tanh and ReLU (panel 1 of Figure 9.7). With sigmoid, the first layers barely move, so the network cannot learn.






Figure 9.8: Top: sigmoid, tanh and ReLU (solid) and their slopes, the derivatives (dashed, shaded), as in Session 8. Bottom: backpropagation multiplies one slope per layer, so the gradient that reaches a weight \(n\) layers back from the output is scaled by the product of \(n\) slopes (the weights, which also enter the product, are left out here). With sigmoid, even the best case leaves 0.00024 after six layers. With tanh, how much is lost depends on how far units are from \(z = 0\), while ReLU passes the whole gradient through active units.




Fix. Change what the gradient has to pass through. The options are ReLU-like activations, initialisation scaled to each layer’s size, standardised inputs, normalisation layers such as batch normalisation (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015), and, in later sessions, residual connections. Adam (below) gets the sigmoid network to 0.291 by enlarging the tiny steps, but that is a workaround, not a cure, because the gradients still vanish.

ReLU (Session 8) never shrinks the gradient for positive inputs, which is why it is the default for hidden layers. Its flat side, however, can leave a unit with no gradient at all (“dying ReLU”, the first discussion problem). Vanishing gradients come back in very deep CNNs (Session 10), recurrent networks and Transformers (Session 11), and each of those sessions shows the architectural fix.


9.5.3 Failure 3: the optimiser and the learning rate

Observation. The same 64/64 network reaches a validation MAE of 0.250 with Adam (learning rate 0.001), but only 0.305 with plain SGD in the same 20 epochs. With Adam and a learning rate of 0.1, the error jumps around and never gets below 0.298.
Why? The learning rate sets the step size of gradient descent (Session 1). A rate that is too small is slow, and one that is too large overshoots the minimum. Plain SGD also uses the same step size for every weight, which Adam does not (next subsection).
Fix. Start with Adam and a learning rate around \(10^{-3}\), and always watch the validation curve.



9.5.4 Momentum and Adam: why an optimiser can beat plain stochastic gradient descent
Plain SGD takes each step straight down the gradient of the current mini-batch. This becomes a problem in a long, narrow valley of the loss, which is common because some weights affect the loss far more than others. In such a valley the gradient points mostly across the valley. A learning rate large enough to make progress along the valley makes SGD zigzag from wall to wall, while a safe one only crawls. The three optimisers differ in how they deal with this:

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) follows the current gradient.
Momentum follows an average of the recent gradients, like a heavy ball rolling downhill. Directions that agree from step to step add up, and the zigzag across the valley cancels out.
Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) combines momentum with a separate step size for every weight, scaled to the size of that weight’s recent gradients. Its default learning rate of \(10^{-3}\) works for many networks.







Figure 9.9: Three optimisers, 60 steps each, on a valley 100 times steeper across (\(w_2\)) than along (\(w_1\)). SGD zigzags and then crawls (loss 0.09 after 60 steps); momentum (0.0004) and Adam (0.006) reach the minimum.



How Adam sets a step for each weight. For every weight, Adam keeps two running averages over the recent mini-batches: \(m\), the average gradient \(g\) (the momentum), and \(v\), the average squared gradient. After each mini-batch it updates them and then the weight:
\[
m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1)\,g, \qquad
v \leftarrow \beta_2 v + (1-\beta_2)\,g^2, \qquad
w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{m}{\sqrt{v} + \epsilon}.
\]
The defaults are \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), which averages over roughly the last 10 steps, \(\beta_2 = 0.999\), roughly the last 1,000 steps, and a tiny \(\epsilon\) that prevents division by zero. Dividing by \(\sqrt{v}\) is the key step. If a weight’s gradient keeps the same sign, \(m/\sqrt{v}\) is close to 1, so the weight moves by about \(\eta\) per step, whatever the size of its gradient. A weight with tiny gradients, like those in the first layers of the deep sigmoid network of Failure 2, therefore takes steps as large as a weight with large gradients. If a weight’s gradient keeps changing sign, as across the valley in Figure 9.9, the positive and negative gradients cancel in \(m\) and the weight barely moves. (Adam also corrects \(m\) and \(v\) for starting at zero, which matters only in the first steps.)
A short history. Adam is the latest step in a long line of ideas (Table 9.2). Gradient descent itself is almost two centuries old. The two ideas that Adam combines, momentum and a separate step size for each weight, were developed separately, and Adam’s contribution was to put them together with sensible defaults.



Table 9.2: Optimisers for gradient descent, from Cauchy to AdamW.










Year
Method
The idea




1847
Gradient descent (Cauchy)
Step downhill along the gradient; proposed for solving systems of equations in astronomy


1951
Stochastic approximation (Robbins & Monro)
Steps based on noisy estimates of the gradient still reach the minimum if the step size shrinks over time: the theory behind SGD


1964
Momentum, the “heavy ball” (Polyak)
Follow an average of the recent gradients, so that consistent directions build up speed


1986
Backpropagation (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams)
Gradients for every weight of a multi-layer network, trained with gradient descent plus momentum


2011
AdaGrad (Duchi, Hazan & Singer)
A separate step size for each weight: divide by the square root of the sum of all its past squared gradients. Rare features get large steps, but all steps shrink towards zero over time


2012
RMSProp (Hinton, in a lecture course; never published as a paper)
Replace AdaGrad’s sum by a running average, so that the steps no longer die out


2015
Adam (Kingma & Ba)
RMSProp’s step sizes plus momentum, with a correction for the start; it became the default, and the paper is one of the most cited in all of science


2019
AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter)
Apply weight decay (Section 9.8.2) directly to the weights instead of through the gradient, where Adam’s division by \(\sqrt{v}\) would weaken it; the usual choice for training Transformers (Session 11)






Adam is a good default, not a universal winner. In the figure, tuned momentum ends even lower, and which optimiser wins depends on the learning rate and the training time. The lab repeats all three failures on blood-cell images, including this comparison, with one rule: change one thing, see what happens, explain why.

section: 9.6 When a hidden layer pays off: epistasis in a protein
text:
9.6 When a hidden layer pays off: epistasis in a protein
The data. GB1 is a small domain of protein G, a bacterial protein that binds antibodies (IgG). Wu et al. (2016) made all 20⁴ = 160,000 combinations of amino acids at four of its positions (V39, D40, G41 and V54), and measured by deep sequencing how well each variant binds IgG. Of these, 149,361 variants have a value. Fitness is relative to the wild type (VDGV = 1) and spans several orders of magnitude, so we predict \(\log_{10}(\text{fitness} + 0.001)\). Each variant is described by the one-hot encoding of its four residues (Session 7), that is, by 4 × 20 = 80 numbers.
Additive or not? A linear model on this encoding gives every amino acid at every position its own weight and adds them up. It is therefore an additive model, exactly like a profile or PSSM (Session 5), in which each position contributes on its own. Such a model cannot represent epistasis, where the effect of a mutation depends on which residues sit at the other positions. Epistasis is the non-additive, XOR-like pattern of Session 7, now as a measured property of a real protein, and a hidden layer can represent it.
We train the models with early stopping on 20,000 variants, with 5,000 for validation and 20,000 for testing:

The network explains about 79% of the variance in fitness, against 50% for the additive model. Weight decay and dropout help a little, and a network ten times larger does not help further.






Figure 9.11: Left and middle: predicted against measured \(\log_{10}\) fitness for the 20,000 test variants (colour: how many variants fall in each hexagon). The additive model compresses the predictions into a narrow band and misses the fit variants; the network follows the diagonal. Right: test \(R^2\) against the number of training variants.



The network needs data to learn the interactions. With 500 training variants the two models are equally good (\(R^2\) 0.43 against 0.41). The interactions exist, but there are too few examples to learn them. From a few thousand variants on, the network pulls away (0.72 at 5,000, 0.82 at 60,000), while the additive model is stuck at about 0.49, however much data it gets. No amount of data lets a sum represent an interaction.
This is Session 7’s lesson, now on real biological data. A hidden layer can represent non-additive relationships, and with enough data, training actually finds them. It is also the limitation of profiles noted in Session 5, since a sum over positions cannot capture interactions, and Session 12 returns to it with pairwise models learned from multiple alignments. The second discussion problem asks where the advantage comes from, by giving the linear model hand-made interaction features for each pair of positions, as Session 7 did for XOR with \(x_1 x_2\).

section: 9.7 Why not make the network enormous?
text:
9.7 Why not make the network enormous?
If larger networks can represent more, why not always use an enormous one? Session 8’s protein-localisation network answers that question. It has 3000 inputs (150 residues, one-hot), a hidden layer of 64 units and 5 outputs, 192,389 weights in all, and it is trained on only 486 proteins of the homology-aware split.






Figure 9.12: Training and validation accuracy of the localisation network per epoch. Training accuracy reaches 1.0 within a few epochs; validation accuracy peaks at 0.486 (epoch 5) and then falls.



Training accuracy reaches 1.000, so the network memorises every training protein. Validation accuracy, in contrast, peaks at 0.486 after five epochs and then falls, to 0.438 by epoch 29. This is overfitting in its plainest form. With far more freedom than data, the network learns the idiosyncrasies of the training sequences instead of the general signal.
Moreover, the simple baseline wins, as the test set (used once) shows:
